# THE FIRST BOOK OF THE STEGANOGRAPHY
## OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS TO THE MOST SERENE
### PRINCE, THE LORD PHILIP,
### COUNT PALATINE OF THE RHINE,
### DUKE OF BAVARIA,
->and Elector of the Holy Empire, etc.<-

It is the opinion of the most profound men that the most ancient sages, whom they are accustomed to call "philosophers" in the Greek tongue, hid whatever secrets of nature or Art they discovered through various methods and figures, lest they fall into the knowledge of wicked men. The doctors of the Jews also confirm that Moses, the most famous leader of the Israelite nation, did not reveal the ineffable secrets of mysteries in simple words when describing the creation of Heaven and Earth. Furthermore, among our own most learned men, Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> affirms that almost innumerable mysteries lie hidden in the Apocalypse of John <note>The Book of Revelation</note>. The sages of the Greeks, who were held in no small esteem among their own people, did the same. Moreover, our own most learned philosophers and poets, who devoted their efforts to composing fables, delivered one thing to the unskilled and another to the erudite through the same sequence of narrative by a sagacious invention. As a most devoted lover of Wisdom, even if I cannot imitate these men due to the slowness of my own wit, I nevertheless admire them, and because I am able, I do not neglect to read them with the greatest diligence. For when I consider that they devised great things by their own study for the welfare of men, I constrain myself with a certain force and grow fervent, pushing myself toward some imitation, however recent, of those who came before. Nor, as I believe, has this opinion entirely deceived me. Indeed, I have learned many things through continuous study of reading which I did not know before, and I have unlocked an entrance for the reader to investigate more secret and more inclined mysteries through my thoughts. For even if not...

<summary>Johannes Trithemius opens his treatise on secret writing by justifying the use of codes and allegories, citing the precedents of Greek philosophers, Moses, and St. Jerome. He argues that profound truths must be hidden from the "wicked" and "unskilled" to preserve their sanctity.</summary>

<meta>The catchword "ma" suggests continuity with a following page beginning with that syllable. This page serves as a formal dedication and a warning regarding the secrecy of the cryptographic or "steganographic" methods being introduced.</meta>

<note>The left side of this page is partially obscured by a watermark from the Vatican Apostolic Library.</note>

...is of such great condition or industry, that I could or would dare to profess that I have entirely grasped that method of the ancient sages for concealing mysteries. Nevertheless, I have discovered certain similar and varied modes, not entirely foreign to those you will see me conform to, which my mind employs with the most secret intention. By these means, I can communicate this art—which I wish to be spread as widely as possible—to an extraordinary degree and without any suspicion or detection by anyone, whether through open messengers or letters. 

And I did not create the invention of this most secret art so much at the instance of the most Serene Prince, Lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and Prince Elector of the Holy Roman Empire—always the most invincible lover of philosophers, most wise, and most peaceful—because he is the same as my own wishes. To him, I have deservedly commended that this great secret be revealed, and not without the greatest labors have I compiled it into this, his volume. 

I have considered it my reasoning that the most noble things should not be offered to the common crowd of the unskilled, or especially to perverse men. Thus, I have directed this work (which teaches mysteries) toward the understanding of mysteries in such a way that no one from the number of the unskilled—no one, I say, unless he be a most diligent student who has studied this science with the utmost accuracy—shall be able to penetrate fully to our intention by his own virtue, unless he receives it from a teacher. This method of transmission the Hebrews call <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>original: "Cabalam"; here referring to the oral tradition or "reception" of secret knowledge</note>, which is placed over the most hidden mysteries. 

The knowledge of this most secret art, if divulged to the wicked and the reprobate, would harm the Commonwealth <note>original: "Reipubl:"</note> no less than it would benefit the good. For indeed, just as good and religiously studious men use every aid from this source for the good and the common utility, so the evil and reprobate hunt for opportunities—not only from evil things but even from good and most holy institutions—by which they may become worse. Beware, therefore, of this most secret and otherwise useful gift given to the Commonwealth, lest by this most close assistance it should happen... so that just as it offers itself as an instrument to good and holy men for the best...

<summary>The author dedicates his secret methods of communication to Prince Philip, Count Palatine, while warning that this "Kabbalistic" knowledge must be kept from the unworthy to prevent its misuse by the wicked.</summary>
<keywords>Philip Count Palatine, cryptography, secrecy, Kabbalah, Duke of Bavaria, ancient mysteries, transmission of knowledge</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the author's defense and explanation of his steganographic methods, focusing on the security of the system and its accessibility to users of varying skill levels.</meta>

Thus, let the ministry <note>original: "ministerium"; here referring to the service or application of the art</note> provide for the wicked and the impious toward their crimes. For what if some good man and lover of honesty should make known the fruit of his will for the private or common good to another who knows this art, whenever and as often as he wishes? And if he should be struck by the suspicion of any mortal, he can signify through his letters—opening or closing them copiously, with total integrity, and quite openly to all—in such a way that no one, however learned or curious, is able to suspect anything of the sender's secret. Nor, even if it were suspected, can it be detected at any time. <gloss>That is, by himself and through others</gloss> Every connection is slippery and multiform. For this reason, one who has attained this art will soon possess a command of Latin <note>original: "Latinitatem"</note> which he could scarcely achieve with a teacher in two days at the very longest. Now, henceforth, he will write letters in the Latin language with proper composition, clear in whatever narrative, beautiful and sufficiently ornate, to me or to another skilled in this art, by which the intention of his will is made known to me or to the man himself. These mysteries, subject to the <term>Cabalistic</term> <note>The author uses "Cabalistic" here not in the strictly Jewish mystical sense, but to refer to a system of secret encoding or spiritual science</note> virtue, are penetrable by no one, however learned or studious, who is without the art; concerning which even divine spirits might prevail. Now, henceforth, the learned and the unlearned shall write. Man and woman, boy and old man, the good and the bad, the prudent and the playful, in Latin or in any language known throughout all regions of the world, shall write letters in Latin, Greek, or foreign tongues, lacking all suspicion <gloss>namely</gloss> <unclear>innocuous</unclear> to those who do not know, showing one thing in the open, and to others who know, showing the secret. Nor would the safe faith between spouses contracted by oath remain hereafter if this science were made public to the wicked. Indeed, even if one has been ignorant of the Latin language until now, through honest and most holy "childish" words of any language or idiom, now sufficiently...

<summary>The author describes a cryptographic system that allows anyone—regardless of age, gender, or education—to hide secret messages within seemingly innocent Latin or Greek letters. He claims the method is so secure that it cannot be detected by the uninitiated, though he warns of the dangers if such power fell into the hands of the wicked.</summary>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the ethical implications and spiritual mechanics of secret writing, likely following an introductory section on the method's efficacy.</meta>

The aforementioned words will allow the evil and immodest mind and intention of a lover or fornicator to be understood most broadly, even while someone else is present and praising the letters as excellent. In the same way, one can send back a single desire—as far and wide as one wishes—most secretly using those same letters or others, arranged in a public and sufficiently ornate sequence. 

Indeed, although this invention is excellent in itself and quite useful in practice, nevertheless, if it should come to the knowledge of the wicked—which may God forbid—the order of the entire Commonwealth <note>original: "Reipub." or Respublica; referring to the state or organized society</note> could be greatly disturbed over the course of time. Public trust would be endangered, and all letters, legal instruments, writings, and even the very speech of men would fall under the gravest suspicion. No one would then believe in letters, however holy and honest, without fear, and would rarely place faith in epistles. For no matter how honest and virtuous the words might be, it would be thought that trickery, fraud, and deception always lay beneath them. Men would become so fearful—no less toward friends than toward adversaries—as to be entirely full of suspicion. 

Nor can anyone, even if he lived for a thousand years, become so learned and expert in this secret doctrine of writing that there would not remain for others infinite, most hidden, and most secret ways within this very art of writing. These methods, working according to the will of any expert student, suggest themselves to all—methods which the student and his teacher have not yet even grasped. 

For since the spirits of the air <note>The "aerei spiritus" are central to Trithemius's system, acting as messengers who convey information across distances.</note>, both good and evil, were created by the Most High God for our service and progress—and through whose intelligence all these holy arts are revealed—they are to us infinite in number and incomprehensible in their virtues. Thus, these arts of ours, which we call **Steganography** <term>Steganography: from the Greek 'steganos' (hidden) and 'graphein' (to write); the art of hiding a message within another message</term> or secret hidden things and mysteries (which are perfectly and holily contained within it), can never be fully exhausted in all their modes, differences of quality, and operation, not even unto eternity, by any mortal, no matter how much judgment or erudition they possess.

<summary>Trithemius warns that while steganography is a powerful tool, its misuse by the wicked could destroy social trust and communication; he further explains that the art is inexhaustible because it is revealed by an infinite number of aerial spirits.</summary>
<keywords>steganography, ethics of secrecy, social trust, aerial spirits, divine revelation, cryptography, Johannes Trithemius</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory framing of the work, moving from the theoretical nature of the "science" to a formal defense of the author's orthodoxy and intent.</meta>

# Prologue

It will be proven otherwise. There is in this science an infinite and most useful Chaos <note>The author uses "Chaos" here to describe a vast, unformed potentiality or a primordial source of knowledge</note>, which no one can perfectly comprehend; for however learned and experienced they may be in this art, you have grasped less than a seventh part, because that is what remains. This profound and most secret art has this property: it easily renders the student incomparably more learned than the teacher, provided he is disposed by nature to <gloss>perceive</gloss> these <gloss>spirits</gloss>. And in these matters, which shall come forth through Cabalistic tradition <note>original: "traditione cabalystica"; referring to the reception of mystical or esoteric knowledge</note>. 

But lest any reader of this art should think—when in the following book I show the names, offices, orders, differences, properties, prayers, and any other operations of the spirits, through whose intelligences all these secrets are perfected—and should establish or assert that I have practiced Necromancy <note>The conjuration of the dead or demonic magic</note> and magic, or have contracted a pact with Demons, or believe me to use or have used any other superstition, I have deemed it necessary and opportune to clear my reputation and name from such a hostile stain, fault, and blot, by claiming the truth for myself through a solemn protestation in this prologue. 

Therefore, before God and the entirely Almighty God, from whom nothing at all can be hidden, and as if in the presence of JESUS CHRIST his only-begotten son, who is to judge the living and the dead, I say in truth—nay, I even protest—that all and singular things which I have said or am about to say in this work, and all properties of the science or art, the methods, figures, or operations, traditions, receptions, formations, inventions, institutions, alterations, and everything which pertains to its speculation, invention, construction, operation, and practice, either in part or in whole, and all things contained in this our volume, rest upon true Catholic and natural principles. They all and individually stand with God, with a good conscience, without hostility to the Christian faith, with the integrity of ecclesiastical tradition; without any superstition whatsoever, without Idolatry, and without any pact with evil spirits.

<summary>The author defends the spiritual legitimacy of his work, claiming that his "Cabalistic" methods for interacting with spirits are based on natural and Catholic principles rather than forbidden necromancy or demonic pacts.</summary>
<keywords>Chaos, Cabalistic tradition, Necromancy, defense of faith, spirits, divine law, ecclesiastical tradition</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's formal declaration (Protestatio), establishing his religious credentials and the moral safety of his work. He emphasizes that his "invention" (the steganographic system) is free from demonic influence and aligns with his monastic vows.</meta>

explicitly and implicitly: without superstition, adoration, veneration, worship, sacrifice, or offering to demons, and without any fault or sin, whether venial or mortal; all and singular things are performed with truth, rectitude, sincerity, and purity. And that the knowledge and practice of this invention does not lead a wise and faithful Christian to such [sinful] use. For I too am a Christian, and voluntarily devoted to the monastic life <note>The author refers to his "monastic conversation," meaning his way of life as a monk</note>, desiring to live and conduct myself in no other way than what befits a true Christian and a monk professed under the Rule of God the Father, Saint Benedict. I have received the Catholic faith itself according to the tradition of the Holy Roman Church, having been baptized in the cradle in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Together with the Holy and Universal Church, I hold and believe this faith, and as long as I live, with God’s help, I strive to keep it always inviolate and firm in heart, word, and deed. Nor do I intend to deviate from it on any occasion.

Far be it from me, therefore—let it be absent—to learn or to teach anything that is contrary to the Christian faith and piety, harmful to holy morals, or in any way adverse to my professed Rule. I fear God and grow old in His worship, from whom I shall be separated neither in life nor in death. I have placed this declaration <note>original: "protestatio"</note> of mine before this work not without cause, especially since we have known many distinguished men who, because they cannot understand what we have written, have turned to insult and have associated our good and holy studies with evil arts and superstitious inventions, and have mocked them. And therefore, we earnestly entreat those who are to come, and all who shall read these our compositions <note>original: "synthemata," referring to his coded arrangements or systems</note>, that if they understand this our holy tradition, they keep the secrets hidden in private. Nor should they pour out such pure mysteries into the public for a long time. If, however, they do not understand (which we know many will not), let them learn before they condemn. A rash judge shows himself to be reckless when he pronounces a sentence on the accused before he knows the truth of the cause. Learn this art first and judge afterward; for if they do not understand it at all, they should not [condemn] it.

<summary>The author, a Benedictine monk, provides a solemn oath that his cryptographic work is free from magic or sin, warning readers to keep its secrets private and urging critics to understand the system before judging it.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Trithemius, Rule of St. Benedict, Protestatio, cryptography, Catholic faith, monasticism, anti-superstition, secrecy</keywords>

...because they <note>Referring to the "good and holy studies" mentioned on the previous page</note> are good; instead, blame your own dull wits. For I know that there are certain ways this work of ours can be criticized, but only by those who happen to be entirely ignorant of it. As for those to whom wisdom is familiar: I neither hope for them to know what we have provided, nor do I wish them to penetrate these mysteries of ours <note>The author implies that the truly wise will already understand his intent, while he actively discourages the unworthy from trying to uncover his secrets</note>.

## CHAPTER ONE

In this first chapter of this first book is contained the standing and operation of the principal spirit **PAMERSIEL**. **Amoyr**, **Madriel** through the most invincible **EBRASA THEAN**. **Abrihel**, **Terasiel**, **Naoros**, **Ormenu**, **Itiller**, **Rathion**, **Namorphiel**. To this end, let there be a commissioning of all with their practice. And the first [operation] of this first chapter is very difficult and full of danger on account of the pride and rebellion of its spirits, who do not yield to anyone unless he is most expert in this art. To novices and those less proven in this art, they not only fail to obey, but even, if they are pressed too hard, they frequently harm them and offend them with various illusions. They are more malicious and unfaithful than all other <term>aerial spirits</term> <note>In the hierarchy of the time, aerial spirits were thought to inhabit the lower atmosphere; they were considered fickle and more likely to interact with—or deceive—humans than higher celestial spirits</note>; and they obey absolutely no one unless compelled by the greatest <term>sacraments</term> <note>original: "sacramentis"; here referring to powerful ritual oaths or holy names used to bind a spirit to service</note>, and they often unfaithfully reveal to others the secret <note>original: "sanctum"</note> entrusted to them. For as soon as they have been sent out with messenger letters to the one they are sent to, they break in without order, like a people fleeing from battle without a leader; fierce as they hurry and filling the air with their clamor, they often manifest the secrets of the sender in a public gathering <note>original: "conventu"</note>. We advise, therefore, that no one intending to work in this art should compel these spirits, nor anxiously seek their services, because they are insolent and unfaithful, especially since one can find many others among those we shall mention later who are sufficiently benevolent and offer themselves up ready for obedience. If, however, anyone wishes to experience their insolence and test those things which we have said...

<summary>Trithemius introduces the spirit Pamersiel and his subordinates, warning that they are exceptionally rebellious, dangerous for beginners, and prone to exposing secrets.</summary>
<keywords>Pamersiel, aerial spirits, messenger spirits, ritual safety, cryptographic spirits, Ebrasathean, Book I</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for communicating via the spirit Pamersiel. ...let him know that this method must be observed. Let him prepare the paper on which he is to write <gloss>is</gloss> with an invocation of the divine name: "In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit" <note>original: "in Nomine patris Filij & Spiritus Sancti." Trithemius often uses orthodox Christian prayers as a "cover" for his cryptographic keys</note>. Then let him write upon it whatever narrative he wishes, simple and open, which all readers may understand, whether in the Latin language or his native tongue <note>original: "patrio sermone," referring to the vernacular language of the writer, such as German or French</note>, or in whatever other language he pleases. However, when he has sat down to write and the spirit compels him to it, [he shall say:]

**PAMERSIEL** Ochmimi, delmison, rasslom, peano, Caristim, Melany, Lyammitto, coleam, prasoys madin Meerlay, Brihre, Alcor, Don, Mikonie, pelgm, Ebriel Alcon, Myrorothalmi, Driaco, person, Crujolnay, Lemo Assosle, midar theariel pean ralsmo Asophel flino hreon, Bariel, Verimos, Exterior Vachina Bestora Tillaomor, Franian Bellodraim, Bon, Otalmergo Me katas, Elmasson Bofranoht. <note>These strange names are "barbarous words" common in magic, but in Trithemius's system, they often serve as a null-cipher or a key. The recipient would look at specific letters within these words to find the hidden message</note>

¶ When he has spoken these things, he will see that the spirit presents himself ready to obey. Let him continue the work he has begun; but if they <note>the spirits</note> appear too slowly, let him repeat the aforementioned words until they appear, or let him stop entirely. Lest, being too greatly compelled, they harm the operator. When he has completed the letters he began, let him send them by <gloss>through</gloss> a messenger to a friend who is skilled in this art. When the friend has received them, let him say this <term>Commination</term> <note>A "commination" is a formal threat or command; here, it acts as the "trigger" for the recipient to begin decoding the message</note>.

Lamarthon, Amisoylon, Madriel, prashon, Ebraso, thea, Panthrenon, Nasintzos, Cameron, Strasbier, Rubanthi, Nadirco Calmosy, Oxmemi, Zamisrules, Damim, Ration, Gamorphin.

¶ Having said these things, the spirit will soon perfectly understand your mind, as those words [the hidden meanings] now present themselves spontaneously with force and cry out, so that clearly others <note>specifically, the intended recipient</note> may perceive the present writing of the sender. But let it be observed in all letters...

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for communicating through the "spirit" Pamersiel. Trithemius is explaining that the "spirit" acts as a cryptographic key. The recipient must understand which spirit is being invoked to correctly decode the message; otherwise, the "spirits" (the cipher system) will fail to reveal the secret and may lead the user into error.</meta>

[the things] which you send, written by this art, mark their own proper sound. So that he to whom you write may know through which spirits the operation is <term>effected</term>. For if he himself <insert><unclear>wishes</unclear></insert> a rash attempt at understanding, and does not attend to it through others <note>The "others" here refers to the specific spirits or keys assigned to the message</note>, they would in no way obey him. Rather, on account of an improper operation, they would both harm him and by no means reveal their secret. For all spirits which we use in this art maintain only the ranks and offices committed to them, and in no way meddle in others. Consider

diligently all that we have said in this present Chapter, and you will be able more easily to understand those things which we are about to say in the following ones. And so that we may prove what we have said with an example, let us set our intention in the common speech or, if you please, in Latin, which we shall subsequently signify to a friend in the manner aforesaid. As if it were the secret intention of some prince’s mind, which he desires his absent <term>vassal</term> <note>A feudal tenant or subordinate who owes service and loyalty to a lord</note> to know.

> Let it be known to us and through us, that for just causes we have decreed that the City of **Strasbourg** <note>original: "Argentinensem," the Roman name for the city of Strasbourg</note> is to be invaded and attacked with the greatest army and power at the next **feast of Vitus and Modestus** <note>The feast day of Saints Vitus and Modestus occurs on June 15th</note>. Wherefore we desire from you that, with the oath and loyalty of your servants by which you are bound to us, you appear on the forenamed day, armed to your best ability, at the fourth hour after noon before the aforementioned City, in the forest standing not far from it, and await our decision on whatever further work needs to be done. Nor should you reveal this purpose of ours to any man. That which is mercifully and benevolently accepted by you, we shall compensate with our grace.

To notify the **vassal** of this **secret**, those things intended to be sent should be written thus, or in another way.

<meta>This page follows the example of the secret message regarding the invasion of Strasbourg. Trithemius now explains how to mask that secret message using a "simple and open" cover text—in this case, a pious prayer—which acts as the carrier for the hidden information.</meta>

> Almighty eternal God, who created all things from nothing, have mercy on us, through the most loving passion of your only-begotten son dying on the cross. Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit without male intervention. Born from the most pure ever-virgin Mary, and voluntarily delivered for us into death. Hear us, etc. <note>original: "Omnipotens æterne Deus... Exaudi &c." This prayer serves as a "cover text." To an outside observer, the letter appears to be a simple religious petition, but it contains a hidden message encoded within its letters.</note>

Write a simple and open narrative of this kind, or any other you wish, which all who read it may understand. And because it contains nothing of a secret nature, you may wish it to come into the sight of everyone <note>This is the essence of <term>steganography</term>: hiding a secret message in plain sight within a non-suspicious document</note>. Write the aforementioned words on paper before the said <term>conjuration</term> <note>In this context, a "conjuration" is likely a specific string of characters or a "key" that tells the recipient how to decode the message</note> with your face turned toward the east. Because once written, you may express your secret intention, whatever you wish, whether in the absence or the presence of spirits. Calling upon them to act faithfully, they will immediately obey. When indeed you know the recipient has received it from the sender, and immediately upon recognizing the sign of the east, with your face turned toward the east, say the conjuration which we have set forth:

->**Lamarthon Angiras**<-

*and immediately he will understand your secret intention which you committed to the spirits to be delivered to him.*

### Locations of the Spirits.

But, since it is especially necessary for everyone working in this <term>science</term> <note>Trithemius refers to his system of cryptography as a "science," though he masks it in the terminology of magic</note> to know the locations and names of the principal Spirits, and their signs, lest through ignorance one should call a spirit dwelling in the south from the **North** <note>original: "Aquilone," the Roman term for the North Wind or the North</note>. Which would not only hinder the intent, but could also harm the practitioner <note>In the "magic" layer, this means demonic retribution; in the "cryptographic" layer, it means the message will be garbled and undecipherable if the wrong key or table is used</note>. I will therefore set down for you in a circle the regions in which the principal Spirits dwell, along with their names and signs.

# CHAPTER TWO.

The prince of this chapter is called **PADIEL**, of the **East Wind** <note>original: "Subsolanis" — referring to the wind blowing from beneath the sun, i.e., the East.</note>, having under him 10,000 day-servants, 20,000 night-servants, and many other sub-servants, whose number is uncertain. For as was said in the preceding chapter, **Pamesiel** with his spirits is entirely relentless and untrustworthy, nor does he readily obey everyone desiring to work in this art, but only the most expert, and even then it is difficult to attempt without danger. However, in this present chapter, we wish to provide a safer way and to demonstrate the method of operating in this art through better spirits, who are benevolent, prompt, and cheerful when called to obedience. When summoned in the proper manner and time, they will come without delay, and whatever is committed to them, they will faithfully carry out without any deceit.

->The Veil: A Secret which is committed not to letters,<-
->but to the spirits of the **second mansion**.<-
<note>The "second mansion" refers to a specific rank or station in the spiritual hierarchy described in this grimoire.</note>

Suppose someone has been reported to a Prince, accused of some crime, such as <term>lèse-majesté</term> <note>original: "laesae maiestatis" — a crime of "injured majesty" or treason against the ruler.</note> or any other matter. The first person [the Prince] wishes to contact the offended party, from whom he is separated by a great distance. However, he does not wish to write to him personally, lest—if the letter were intercepted by any chance—the accused criminal might flee, or resist by gathering the strength of his friends, or someone else might act sinisterly against the prince and the laws. He writes this letter (or another narrative of the grievance) to the intended official, which he does not fear to have read by anyone. But the **Secret** he commits to a spirit in the manner we have previously described, who will faithfully relate his secret to the one to whom he sends it, provided that person is already instructed in this art. With sincere honesty, namely through prayer and penitential devotion, quite beautifully composed and brief, and with the full goodwill of my mind, he does not wish to possess it alone; and it is such:

->CHAPTER III<-

The Prince of the third chapter is **CAMUEL**, located in the East; he has under him spirits presiding over daily operations and nightly ones, specifically, with ten subservient spirits. Their duty is to manifest assistance in many ways through spirits who are otherwise very venerable and suited for achieving designated goals, for all those who work in the proper form within this <term>science of the saints</term> <note>original: "scientia sanctorum" — a term used in grimoires to describe the sacred art of theurgy or ritual magic as a holy endeavor.</note>. He has few ministers here, but they are voluntary, good, and faithful, up to 10 day spirits and 10 night spirits. They are always sent one or two at a time for an operation from each order. These day spirits do not create darkness, and those who preside over the night do not create light. Wherever necessity demands in every commission, one joins with the other. When they appear visibly, they are all seen in beautiful clothing mixed with Glory, and another is accustomed to stand by in a garment of shining splendor. Often, however, they appear only by a sensible effect <note>A "sensible effect" means the spirit's presence is felt by the senses—such as a change in temperature or a feeling in the air—rather than being seen with the eyes.</note>, but they are not seen unless it so pleases the practitioner.

That **CAMUEL**, with his ministers and subordinates, holds authority and the truth of announcing the state, will, and condition of an absent friend—the path, the travels, the arrival and the return—whenever the practitioner of this art wishes. Therefore, when you wish to work in this art according to his will through the angels of his station <note>original: "mansione" — referring to the spirit's 'mansion' or specific residence within the celestial hierarchy.</note>, you must first know who these Angels of Camuel are, which are the Spirits of the day, and over what each of them is appointed. And likewise for the night spirits. So that you may know this, I have chosen to provide the following table immediately.

# CHAPTER IV

The chief of the fourth chapter is Aseliel; he dwells toward the South-East <note>original: "Euro-Austrum"; a classical term for the wind or direction between the East and South-East</note>, and he has under him 20 substitute princes with their servants. <margin>ASELIEL</margin>
The fourth mansion from the East toward the South-East is held by the great Prince ASELIEL with his spirits. Of these, 10 preside over the daytime operations in this art, and twenty over the nighttime ones. The power and duty of all these is to report those things which pertain to the love of women. Now, these 20 chief spirits have others under them, and they send an equal number in order to their duties when they have been called in the proper manner by the operator. Again, there are others subject to these, of whom there is a great number. For in the art of Steganography <term>Steganography: literally "hidden writing"; here Trithemius uses the names of spirits as a code to hide secret messages within seemingly innocent texts</term>, when working with the prince of the 4th mansion, there is no need to summon all the subject spirits. I shall therefore give the names of a few, along with the number [of servants] subject to them, from which you may always summon one or two, whichever you wish. Nor do you need more, unless the operation is for various purposes.

They [the guards] will praise the writing and show it to the lady to be read. She, recognizing the messenger by the signs, calls the hidden messenger, hears the counsel, and sends back her consent. ### CHAPTER XVII

The principal Spirit <gloss>a</gloss> and supreme Emperor is called **CARNESIEL** <gloss>c</gloss> and he dwells in the east, having under him many dukes, princes, and servants. Their duty is to administer all things <gloss>e</gloss> <note>original: *oia*, an abbreviation for *omnia*</note> which are announced toward the east. Since indeed there are many and various affairs of men that may emerge and need to be communicated, and since none of the aforementioned 16 mansions <note>refers to the spirits described in the previous sixteen chapters</note> is specifically designated for these tasks in a more suitable way, these four were identified through the Author's diligence. This was done so that those practicing this art of <term>Steganography</term> <note>the art of hidden writing, which Trithemius masks here as a system of "angelic" communication</note> might not encounter any difficulty in perfecting the work.

For after special mention was made of certain spirits in the preceding chapters who preside over specific secrets, it is now pleasing to add certain general methods for announcing general matters. Thus, if perhaps a secret to be announced should occur for which no specific assignment <note>original: *commissio*</note> is found in the previously mentioned spirits, it may be referred to these four. These spirits, in their own way, have authority over everything—yet in such a way that a general category <gloss>c</gloss> does not override a specific one, nor should a specific category that is not clearly defined refuse the duty of the general category.

Therefore, there are four great princes who, with their Dukes and sub-servants, preside over all secrets to be announced, as expressed above. Of whom the first, **Carnesiel**, presides over all things we wish to announce toward the east; the second, **Caspiel**, toward the south; **Amenadiel** toward the west; and **Demoriel** toward the north.

<margin>Example 1.</margin>
When, therefore, you wish to announce some secret through friendly spirits as is customary toward the east: call one or more of the princes of **Carnesiel** as you wish. Intending to conduct yourself throughout the whole operation toward the eastern region of the world according to our art...

> The general secret is present for the messengers, whom you have called by their own [names]; a faithful, weighing of secrets. <note>original: *Adest generalis arcanum nunciis, quem vocasti propriis, fidelis, pensoris, secretis.* In Trithemius's system, this Latin sentence often serves as a key or a grammatical template for the hidden message.</note>

<margin>Example</margin>
Suppose there is a certain man of honest appearance who is actually evil, and he knows that I have some influence with a friend. He asks for letters of recommendation to be sent to that friend on his behalf. I do not dare to refuse him. Yet, I do not want my friend to be deceived by this man. ### CHAPTER XXI

<margin>
**Geradiel**
</margin>

**Geradiel** is the prince and Emperor of this chapter, residing in no specific region of the world but wandering everywhere, thus he remains. In addition to those Emperors, Princes, and leaders of Spirits whom we named in the previous chapters—who reside in fixed places and are assigned according to a visible order—there are others who are everywhere wandering and unstable, residing in no fixed place. These the ancient Sages and magi called **Droccos Hefesta** <note>original: "Droccos hefesta"; likely a pseudo-Greek construction by Trithemius meant to imply "lowly" or "earth-bound" wandering spirits</note>, common to all; they fly in the air like flies without order, without a home, and without restriction. Among these are several not useless to us for Steganography <term>Steganography: The art of hidden writing; in this context, Trithemius uses the summoning of spirits as a metaphor for the encryption and transmission of secret messages</term>. This is because they do not require the observation of specific locations, but can be summoned in any place through an Incantation.

The first of these is called **Geradiel**, who does not have any leader or prince beneath him; instead, he has only many servants, almost innumerable, whom he takes with him into service according to the orders they hold among themselves throughout the 24 hours of the day and night. Their general duty is to report secrets to any place in the world you wish, regarding any matter whatsoever.

# CHAPTER XXII

Buriel, a great prince, follows Geradiel in this chapter. He rules <note>original: "permiserit," likely a corruption of a word meaning to govern or preside over</note> seven kingdoms through other spirits, and especially pursues and detests the princes of the earth; and he is no less a devil to them. Each of these is divided along with all their families. Nor is he ever accustomed to come except by night, and this frequently with great horror and fear for those performing the work—especially if the practitioner is not perfect in the art, constant, and brave in spirit.

He frequently appears in the likeness of a serpent, having the head of a Virgin, but the tail and the whole body of a serpent, hissing horribly. Once satisfied in the proper manner, he speaks with human words. He has under him dukes and princes, whom he is accustomed to send into service, along with their families and all other things, the multitude of which is almost innumerable. The Duke is accustomed to appear in the form we have described; however, the servants usually appear frequently as monkeys, or as <term>jugglers (Iugilatores)</term> <note>meaning jesters or entertainers</note> bearing games and leaping from on high to the ground in a marvelous fantasy.

Their office is to announce all nocturnal secrets during the night. And they are willing to perform service in prisons and <note>original: "lacus," literally lakes, but often referring to pits or dungeons</note> pits for captives. And similarly in those matters which pertain to carnal love. He performs these <term>illusions (præstigias)</term>, Amantin. And all things that are done in the night are good without malice, because they hate the light.

## CHAPTER XXIII

**HYDRIEL** is the supreme Prince of this chapter’s title. He dwells in waters, among fishes, in lakes, marshes, and the sea, as well as around springs, cisterns, and rivers. He holds under his dominion those spirits previously mentioned in the preceding chapter regarding their Emperor. The general office of these spirits is to administer all things both by water and by land, whether it be by day or by night. As they are subject to the king’s will and are well-disposed, these princes are ready for all tasks. However, they appear in this form <note>likely referring to the specific ritual manifestation described next</note> when they are summoned under threat. They frequently appear in an **infernal manifestation**. Sometimes they appear as <unclear>aligna</unclear> <note>The Latin here is difficult; it may refer to a sea-creature or siren</note> with the head of a very beautiful virgin and with hair spread out.

## CHAPTER XXIV

**PYRICHIEL** has under him many princes, counts, and servants, the number of whom is uncertain. As a Duke or prince, he rules over others in the manner of the rest, but operates through his Counts and sub-ministers. Otherwise, he is quite benevolent. He took his name from fire <note>original: "ab igne desumpsit," from the Greek *pyr* for fire</note> because he is accustomed to frequently dwell around fire.

## CHAPTER XXV

**EMONIEL** is the supreme prince of this chapter, having under him many Dukes, Counts, and sub-ministers. They have a general office over all things. He is unstable and wandering, and frequently dwells in the groves <note>original: "nemoribus," referring to woods or forested areas</note>. He is not wise <note>original: "Non sapit," implying a lack of higher intellect or discernment</note> although he is benevolent and prompt in all things. He is accustomed to appear with two of his companions, having the head of a virgin, the body of a wild beast, and a serpentine tail.

# CHAPTER XIX

Macariel has 10 princes under his empire. Of these, he never sends fewer than three into service. We send letters, however, for a twofold reason, even though we could announce a secret without letters through a spirit alone: both so that we may free men from suspicion through the received characters <note>The "characters" or letters serve as a mundane "cover" to explain the message's arrival to observers</note>, and so that we may compel the spirit—bound by the character itself—to obey that friend.

### BOOK THE SECOND

<margin>
To the King <note>likely referring to the dedicatee or a specific rank of spirit</note>
14. j. F.
From the library: hand:
Rome
</margin>

In the preceding book, with the supreme help of GOD, I have set in order thirty-one spirits <note>Trithemius refers to the 31 spirits cataloged in Book I of his *Steganographia*, which include 24 spirits of the hours and 7 planetary/directional spirits.</note> through their ranks, the supreme Commanders of our art, and we have arranged them with their two Counts and servants necessary to us for the work, not without great labor. Although their services may suffice abundantly for every practitioner for the communication of secrets, however hidden they may be, nevertheless, lest we seem to omit anything that might contribute to the perfection of the art, we have joined this second book to the first volume. Moreover, since for each individual hour of the day and night there are specific spirits, assigned by the special tradition of the wise to various operations, divine works, and wondrous effects: It pleased us to follow their order, though without imitating superstition, so that we might take from them what serves our purpose without harm to the Christian name. Let us pass over the rest as vain, full of magical superstitions and contrary to our faith. Therefore, for each of the hours, both of the day and of the night, assigned through the secret of Solomon, surnamed Hermes <note>original: "Salomonis cognomento Hermetis"; Trithemius often links King Solomon and Hermes Trismegistus as the legendary founders of the "Ars Notoria" or sacred magic.</note>, in his volume on magic, we shall abundantly attain the principal Spirits as the supreme Commanders of the art, along with the other officials necessary for our proposed operation. And we shall give both the method and the instruction to all students in this art, by which they may be ready to reveal a certain sequence of their dwellings with the Counts at any hour, namely by counsel. For every prince presides over his spirits, Dukes, counts, and servants like an Emperor; called by us according to his instruction with a lawful Song <term>Carmine: literally "song" or "poem," but in this context, it refers to a ritual incantation or the cryptographic "key" disguised as a prayer</term>, they come, deliver the entrusted secrets, and show themselves obedient and strong to us in all things.

<meta>This page begins the detailed instructions for Book Two of the *Steganographia*. ...I am about to make mention, I think I must again declare that nothing in this art is to be considered frivolous, nothing superstitious, nor contrary to Gospel teaching. For all things which we have either said in the preceding book, or are about to say in those following, are supported by natural, lawful, and honorable principles; only to foreign instructions <note>original: "peregrinis institutionibus"; likely referring to the specialized, non-standard methods of his system</note> like mysteries, and words wrapped in names and sentences, do they require a learned reader. For they use the ministry of a spirit to veil the meaning, which they know is published to the wicked. And lest anyone fail through error in the calculation of hours, let them know that we have adopted planetary hours <note>Unlike modern hours of fixed 60-minute lengths, planetary hours vary in duration based on the time between sunrise and sunset, divided into twelve equal parts.</note> both by day and by night.

# CHAPTER ONE

Samael is the principal and supreme Commander <note>original: "Imperator"</note> who presides over the first hour of the day. And under his command he has many Dukes and Counts, whom he sends in this hour with great power to the practitioner skilled in <term>steganography</term> <note>From the Greek *steganos* (hidden) and *graphein* (writing). While appearing to be about summoning spirits, Trithemius uses this as a metaphor for a complex system of encryption.</note>. Moreover, the first hour of the day is to be calculated as a planetary hour starting from sunrise. He also entrusts secrets to them which the aforementioned spirits carry, but if called outside the designated hour, they utterly disdain to come. And note that the leaders and first princes of Samael are rarely sent by him for the service of a summoning, since they perform the duty of accompanying great and nightly illusions of men. The others, however, along with their followers, are specifically assigned to the service of this art, which they cannot perform <note>The printed text of Trithemius reads "nullatenus possunt" (by no means can) here; the manuscript appears to say "mittant" (they may send).</note> without the divine presence. Since these are from the supreme order among spirits, they are accustomed to showing themselves somewhat proud and rebellious to those who summon them. Nor do they easily obey anyone except the most skilled in the art without labor and danger. For they are arrogant and most ready for illusions and mockery. They especially mock and sneer at those whom they find less skilled in the <term>steganographic</term> art. But those whom they find bold, constant, and experienced in this art, they venerate and fear, and they always most promptly obey their commands with trembling and obedience.

He warns that these entities are arrogant and will only obey a highly skilled and "bold" practitioner of the cryptographic arts.</summary>

## CHAPTER VIII

The eighth hour is called *Afafanyim*; its Angel is **Smadach**, who has under his command 10 dukes and 100 counts. Of his servants, there is no number <note>meaning they are countless</note>. All of these are assigned not only to the practice of <term>Steganography: the art of hidden writing or secret communication through spiritual means</term> but also to many other great works. Hermes <note>original: "Hermes de natura Spirituum"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom many occult works were attributed</note> says regarding the nature of Spirits that all those who are obedient and subject to the aforementioned Smadach—both dukes and counts—are accustomed to appear in various transformations at the will of the practitioner: either as men, or as winged beasts, or as serpents, according as they have been commanded by the operator.

## CHAPTER IX

The ninth hour is called *Karron*, and the name of its supreme Angel is **Quabriel**. He has under his command 10 dukes, 100 counts, and innumerable servants. All of these are accustomed to appear in whatever form they wish.

## CHAPTER X

This hour is called *Lamarchon*, and its supreme Emperor is **Oriel**. He has here many dukes and counts who are assigned to the practice of Steganography.

## CHAPTER XI

The eleventh hour is called *Menasijm*, and its supreme Emperor is **Biriel**. He also has many dukes and spirits under his command, through whom there are wonderful things to be found in Steganography and in various experiments.

## CHAPTER XII

## CHAPTER XXIII:

In the first hour of the night, according to the author Stalacho, the supreme ruler of the Angels is Dardaniel, under whose command are many Dukes, Counts, and spirits. The Dukes are benevolent, cheerful, and pleasant beyond measure. They delight in communication and are most obedient to men—specifically to those well-instructed and operating correctly in the art. And it should be noted that the number of these Dukes is infinite, for almost the entire air is filled with them, and they cannot be counted. There are also other evil spirits who run and scurry invisibly among men, always inciting them to evil, and they drag the unwary with them to hell. And through them, infinite wicked deeds <term>maleficia: harmful magic or evil acts</term> are committed, not only among Christians, but also among the infidels.

# CHAPTER XXIV

Its hour is called Zephar, and its superior Angel is Samadiol, who has under his power primary leaders, counts, and many servants. These spirits are accustomed to appear frequently in the form in which the Devil of that law <note>The "law" likely refers to a specific magical system or religious framework being described by the author.</note> is held to have appeared: with a head covered <unclear>with a cap</unclear> like a maiden’s, with hair hanging down on both sides. # CHAPTER XXV

Whoever desires to approach the understanding of this, our occult art <term>occult art</term> <note>At the time of this manuscript, "occult" simply meant "hidden" or "secret" knowledge, often involving the study of nature's unseen forces.</note>, and through it longs to perform wonders, it is necessary first of all that he be adorned with virtues and a clean conscience, with good will toward God and his neighbor; and in no way should he be prone to harming anyone. Nor should he seek the dealings of folly. 

Next, it is necessary that he be learned in books, most highly instructed in the knowledge of the humanities, and especially very well-versed in the science of astronomy <note>In the Renaissance, astronomy and astrology were often studied together as a single discipline to understand the influence of the heavens on Earth.</note>. This is so that he knows their general movements, changes, orders, magnitudes, positions, risings, settings, and the effects of the stars, the Zodiac signs, and the planets. For without a competent knowledge of the stars, no one can have access to the inner secrets of this art.

Consequently, it is necessary that he have a teacher <term>preceptor</term> <note>A mentor or master who provides oral instruction and guidance that cannot be found in books alone.</note> who is perfect and experienced in the art. For we believe it is possible only for a few—and even among many, hardly for the most learned and those most skilled in magic—to come to this science without a teacher. Furthermore, the teacher must be not only proven and experienced in the knowledge of the matter, but also faithful, pious, and God-fearing. For the purer the science is in relation to God, the more successful and secure one will be in the practice of this science; the spirits and the Virtues <note>original: "Virtutibus"; likely referring to the celestial hierarchies or the inherent powers of the universe.</note> obey such a person.

# JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS’S STEGANOGRAPHY BOOK III

After we have completed, with God’s help, the first two books of our art, in which we described both types of steganography <note>original: "steganographiam... utramq̃"; Trithemius likely refers to the two different systems of spirit-based cryptography detailed in Books I and II.</note>; it is necessary for us then to subjoin this third one, and, having added wonderful things, to connect it to more universal principles. I read in a certain ancient book of a philosopher of the Indians, who is said to be Menastor <note>Menastor is a pseudonym or legendary figure often cited by Trithemius; there is no historical evidence of such an Indian philosopher, suggesting he may be a literary device to lend authority to the text.</note>, that it is possible by a certain art to make the concept of our mind known to a friend, however distant, within 24 hours, without words, without letters, and without a messenger, most perfectly, most broadly, and most secretly. Driven by a most vehement desire for knowledge, I began to want to test this truth I had read. And after many labors, I finally found it, proven by science and experience. For it is the greatest secret of the art, and wrapped in such great obscurities that it is not easily accessible to anyone. For Menastor granted it obscurely and to few, as a mystery. He so vividly ensured it remained a secret that I have not yet been able to find anyone after him who dared to make his discourse clearer by any instruction. But I, fearing that such a divine work, because of its excessive obscurity, might either be held in contempt by the unskilled, or finally be burned in fire <note>A common concern for occultists of the period was the destruction of their manuscripts by authorities who might mistake their work for forbidden sorcery.</note>, since I have already experienced many perfections in it, wished to commend it in clearer letters. So that, with God’s help, it might be of some use to learned men and those most studious in the arts <note>original: "magis studiosissimis"; this refers to practitioners of the "higher" or "natural" magics.</note>. And that it should remain hidden from the impious <term>kachoshagos</term> <note>original: "kachoshagos"; a Greek-derived term created by Trithemius, likely from *kakos* (evil) and *magos* (magician), meaning "evil sorcerers."</note>, and in no way known to their darkened intellect.

<summary>Johannes Trithemius introduces Book III, claiming to have rediscovered an ancient Indian method for transmitting thoughts across any distance within twenty-four hours without physical means. He justifies publishing these secrets to prevent the knowledge from being lost or destroyed, while still intending to keep it hidden from "evil" practitioners.</summary>

<keywords>Book III, Menastor, Indian philosopher, long-distance communication, mental transmission, kachoshagos, secret arts, divine work</keywords>

Moreover, Monastros <note>original: "Monaster"; likely a reference to a character or authority within this fictionalized magical dialogue</note> said: There are seven Planets over which seven Angels preside. Thus, at the time of the Great Flood, the wise men held that Samael, the Angel of Mars, was the world’s lord; but Gabriel <note>Angel of the Moon</note> ruled at the time of the confusion of languages <note>The Tower of Babel</note>, 
<margin># Angel of the Moon.</margin> 
and Michael, the Angel of <term>the Sun</term> <note>original: ☉</note>, ruled at the time of Israel’s departure from Egypt. If anyone places faith in the aforementioned assertion, he himself will be able to easily calculate the changes of eras and the governments of the Angels from the origin of the world down to his own age in the prescribed order. 

We, however, pursuing those things which lead to our current purpose, will not doubt that the seven Angels of the planets have other spirits subject to them—the 21 mentioned before—according to the records of our instruction, through whom we work the effects of our intention. We observe the customary order of the Planets, beginning from the highest of all, Saturn, and descending to the Moon. Therefore, first considering the primary operation of each Angel, we will then join the specific Chapters <note>referring to the sub-sections of the magical system</note> of those spirits following him in order.

# CHAPTER ONE

->Concerning the first and highest Angel<-
->of Saturn, Orifiel,<-
->and concerning the operations<-
->which are performed through him.<-

Saturn is the highest and most supreme of all the planets, slow in motion and cold in nature, because it is far removed from the earth. From the point of its beginning until the completion of thirty years—that is, to the point of its first station—it stays in each sign of the zodiac for thirty months. <note>Saturn’s orbit takes approximately 29.5 years; Trithemius is using the standard medieval rounded figure of 30 years.</note> By its near-natural motion, it stays for twenty-eight months and six [days]. Its first and supreme Angel, according to the opinion of the ancients, is called Orifiel. He has under him three other principal spirits, namely Sadach, Samiel, and Morofiel, of whom we shall speak in the proper place. 

Through this great Orifiel, the Angel of Saturn, many and diverse operations are performed in <term>steganography</term> <note>In this context, Trithemius uses "steganography" to mean not just "hidden writing," but a system of spiritual communication where messages are sent via planetary intelligences.</note>. For through him, we are able to make the secret concept of our mind known to a friend who also knows this science, wherever he may be, by letters if desired, or even without letters. Many other wonderful things can also be worked, which no one will understand except one skilled in this science. 

Therefore, one wishing to perform anything in steganography through this Angel, especially on the day of Saturn <note>Saturday</note> regarding things subject to Saturn: first, it is necessary that he knows its diverse and various motions. First the single, the proper, the mixed, the direct, the retrograde, and the <term>stationary</term> <note>original: "consessum," referring to the "station" of a planet when it appears to stand still in the sky.</note>. And in all these, it is necessary to know not only the general rules handed down by astronomers (for although they are highly conducive to this science of ours, they are not entirely sufficient), but also the particular ones.

For the foundation, therefore, with the tables and rules about the planetary motions having been frequently set down—which is absolutely necessary for the practitioner in this art—we have added special rules and tables <gloss>of the Planets</gloss> <insert>and of the hours</insert> of their motions through the individual chapters <insert>or sections</insert> of this book. And <unclear>well</unclear> note that the day of any planet is divided into four equal parts. The principal Angel of that planet governs the first of these, which numbers the first three unequal hours from the rising of the sun. <note>An "unequal hour" (also called a planetary hour) is calculated by dividing the total daylight of a specific day into twelve equal portions. Because the length of the day changes with the seasons, these "hours" are rarely sixty minutes long.</note> The three substitutes of the said principal Angel follow the remaining three quarters of the artificial day <note>The "artificial day" refers to the time from sunrise to sunset, as opposed to the "natural day" of twenty-four hours.</note> in order.

->For example.<-

On the day of Saturn <note>Saturday</note>, Orifiel—the first and principal Angel of that day—possesses for himself the first three unequal planetary hours, calculated from the rising of the sun. The first Angel among the substitutes of Orifiel, who is called Sadael, possesses the second three hours. Boniel, who is otherwise second in the order of Orifiel’s substitutes, holds the third three hours. And the fourth or last three hours are assigned to the third and final substitute, called Manasael.

Thus, in the first hours of the day of Saturn (♄) <note>original: "♄", the astrological symbol for the planet Saturn</note>, in matters pertaining to Saturn <unclear>namely</unclear>, one must work through Orifiel; in the second set of hours, through Sadael; in the third, through Boniel, and so forth. And all operations, according to the measure and <unclear>condition</unclear>, will obtain either a successful or a weak effect. In the same way, on the remaining days, one must work under the individual quarters of the day through their own assigned Angels.

## On the Various Motions of the Planets and the Interpretation of the Tables.

Although in the present chapter we are to have a special discussion concerning the motions of Saturn <note>The symbol ℏ in the original text represents the planet Saturn, the outermost of the seven classical planets.</note> and its spirits, as well as the operations of steganography <note>original: "steganographia"; here referring to Johannes Trithemius’s system of hidden writing which he disguised as a system of planetary magic and spirit communication.</note> p. cor. <note>An abbreviation, likely for "per corda" (through the heart) or a specific technical shorthand used in this manuscript.</note> Lest we be compelled to repeat things appropriately said once in every single chapter, we advise the studious reader that he should strive to be mindful in the following chapters of those things which we say in this chapter.

For there are various motions of each of the planets, and they are most subtly divided into various others. For to us also, their own manifold motion varies from various most subtle divisions. Direct, retrograde, mixed, etc., it enjoys almost as many varying points as are measured from the beginning of its motion in the Circle <note>The "Circle" refers to the ecliptic or the 360-degree path of the zodiac.</note>. What shall I say regarding the combination of these planets with one another? For if Ptolemy says in his *Centiloquium* <note>The *Centiloquium* is a famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to the 2nd-century astronomer Claudius Ptolemy.</note>, there are one hundred and twenty combinations among the planets themselves: namely, 21 pairings [binary], 35 groupings of three [ternary], 35 groupings of four [quaternary], <insert>21 groupings of five, 7 groupings of six, and</insert> one grouping of seven; and we shall speak of these in their proper place.

However, regarding the other motions, although we cannot give a certain limit because of the infinite diversity by which they are varied daily—with the ascendants having been positioned or impending—the full extent being unknown. Nevertheless, as much as we are able to observe, we have found more than 30,000 divisions in which these operations of the art often vary in their effect. And unless someone is highly expert in all these things—namely, the mean motions <term>mean motion: the mathematical average speed of a planet, assuming a perfectly circular orbit</term> of all the planets perfectly, and then the most minute punctual divisions which reach us, handed down with great subtlety from fourths, thirds, seconds, minutes, and degrees—he will easily fall into various errors and will scarcely escape with the grace of knowledge.

Therefore, for the perfect instruction of this **science** <term>scientia; here referring to the specialized knowledge of steganography or hidden communication</term>, we have arranged three **tables**. In the first of these, the motion of **Saturn** <note>represented by the symbol ♄</note>, and in the second, the motion of **Jupiter** <note>represented by the symbol ♃</note>, prove the parts of both the day and the night. For as we have brought the calculation back to the **root** <term>radix; the base value or starting point used in astronomical and cryptographic calculations</term> point and to the true point of the ascendant of any given sign, taking up the arrangement from the first degree of the east, through the promised 641, and through 8 and 700 <note>These numbers likely refer to specific intervals or units in Trithemius's encryption cipher</note>, we take the whole **Zodiac** in the second table by time.

Next, in that same second table, we have described the motion of **Saturn** (in which there are twelve signs) for all four quarters of the day and night. We have recorded this down to the minutes so that at any hour of the night, once the degree of the ascendant in which **Saturn** itself was located is known, its primordial **root** can be clearly revealed. Once, before the **celestial operation** <note>original: "celestiationem"; likely referring to the completion of a ritual or the full calculation of the planetary positions</note> is finished, we say—though I know not if our age is able to attain it—that the Table must be started anew from the head of its own beginning.

In the third table <note>The original manuscript uses "fabula" (story/fable), but the context clearly indicates "tabula" (table)</note>, we have reduced the sevenfold mixture of **Saturn** with the other planets to the proportion of the point, because it is unique. Through this, all things are easily brought back from a distance to the point.

In the same table, the pure motion of the planets is found through every aforesaid division of the same principle, providing the perfection and the distance from the point in any progress of motion, provided that the **mean motion** <term>medius motus; the average speed of a planet, assuming a circular orbit at a constant speed, used as a baseline for astronomical calculations</term> is already fully possessed. For without knowledge of the **mean motion**, it is impossible for anyone to become a practitioner of this wisdom. Indeed, even if you understand the mean and true motion perfectly, it will profit you nothing for the knowledge of this science unless you understand the three prescribed tables at all points of the divisions in the motions of the planets—taken equally from unequal degrees, down to the individual minutes, in their entirety. 

But now let us proceed to the **operations**.

### Concerning the first Angel of **Saturn** <note>represented by the symbol ♄</note>, who is the principal and is called Orifiel; he observes the first quarter of Saturn.

As we have said in the preceding sections, the first principal Angel of **Saturn** <note>♄</note> is Orifiel, who, along with the other angels of the planets, governs the world in his order for 354 years and 4 months. He holds the first quarter in both the day and the night. Through him, the operation is performed from the rising of the **Sun** <note>represented by the symbol ☉</note> during the day, and from its setting at night, up until the third hour inclusive, in all matters that pertain to the Saturnine. This applies within his specific day and night. 

Therefore, when you wish to announce something to someone who is absent during the first quarter of **Saturn** <note>♄</note>—doing so without words <note>original: ✝; a cross-mark likely used here as a shorthand or separator</note> and without letters, but through the spirit of Saturn—you must call upon no other than Orifiel, since through him you will be able to announce all things most perfectly. 

First, consider in which zodiac sign **Saturn** <note>♄</note> is located, and at what degree, and whether it is **direct or retrograde** <note>astronomical terms: "direct" means the planet moves forward through the zodiac, while "retrograde" means it appears to move backward from Earth's perspective</note>. Also, consider which planet it is in conjunction with. Let us set down an example for the first part.

Suppose **Saturn** <note>♄</note> is now at 25 degrees of **Taurus** <note>original: ♉ ♉</note> on the 28th day of April in the year 1500. And now let us say 25 multiplied by 24 <note>original: ✝; the cross-mark here indicates a mathematical operation</note> becomes 600. Divide these by 4 equal quarters, and they give a quotient of 150 for each quarter. Let us complete the degrees of **Saturn** <note>♄</note> in the sign of **Taurus** <note>♉</note>, which are 30. Let us multiply 30 by 25, and they produce 750. Let us **cast away** <note>original: Proijciamus; a mathematical term for subtracting a specific value or a remainder</note> the superfluous degrees from the middle of the third quarter, and 600 will remain. Let us now take the point of Saturn's motion from the table for the present day and hour. Thus we will be able to know the rising, the elevation, and the setting of the Angel Orifiel with **Saturn** <note>♄</note> in the first quarter. All of this knowledge will make our operation easier. The table follows.

# PICATRIX

King Alfonso of Spain <note>original: "Alphonsus Rex Hispaniæ." This refers to Alfonso X of Castile, known as "The Wise" (reigned 1252–1284), a monarch famous for sponsoring translations of scientific and occult works from Arabic into the vernacular.</note>, and of all Andalusia <note>original: "Handalitiæ." A Latinization of al-Andalus, the Muslim-ruled regions of the Iberian Peninsula.</note>, commanded that this book be translated from the Arabic tongue into Spanish with the greatest care and diligence. This was done for the praise and glory of the highest and almighty God, whose nature it is to reveal the secrets of the sciences to those He has predestined, and also for the enlightenment of Latin scholars, who suffer from a scarcity of books published by the ancient philosophers.

It was compiled from 224 books of philosophy, and this most wise philosopher called it by its own name, the *Spanish Picatrix*. It was finished in the year 1256; in the Era of Caesar, 1295 <note>The "Hispanic Era" or "Era of Caesar" was a dating system used in the Iberian Peninsula that begins in 38 BCE.</note>; in the Era of Alexander, 1568 <note>Also known as the Seleucid Era.</note>; and in the Era of the Arabs, 655 <note>The Islamic Hijri calendar.</note>.

->This work is dedicated only to the wise.<-

It establishes the text's pedigree as a compilation of 224 ancient philosophical works translated from Arabic to preserve "secret sciences" for Latin scholars.</summary>
<keywords>Picatrix, Alfonso X of Castile, Andalusia, Arabic translation, astral magic, occult philosophy, medieval dating eras, secret sciences</keywords>

# BOOK I
## On the science of knowing, and in what rank it stands.
### Chapter 1

Know <gloss>O</gloss> most dear brother: that the greatest and most noble gift which **GOD** has given to the people of this world is **KNOWLEDGE** <note>original: "SCIRE." The Latin verb "to know" is used here as a noun, emphasizing the act of knowing as a dynamic power.</note>, because through knowledge, information is gained concerning ancient things, which are the soul of all things in this world. Through it, we understand which causes are most closely related to the causes of other things, and how one thing has a correspondence <note>original: "convenientiam." This refers to the "doctrine of signatures" or "sympathies," the idea that objects in the natural world are spiritually linked to one another and to the stars.</note> with another. It is because of this that all things are what they are, and we see how one thing is elevated after another in a specific order. 

Furthermore, knowledge reveals the place where He, who is the root and principle <term>principium: the foundational source or first cause</term> of the things of this world, exists; through Him all things are dissolved, and through Him all things, new and old, are known. For He is, in truth, the First, and in Him nothing is lacking, nor does He stand in need of any other, since He himself is the First and the cause of all other things, and He receives no qualities from any other. He is not a body <gloss>is</gloss>, nor is He composed of any body, nor is He mixed with any other thing outside of Himself, but He is entirely within Himself. 

And for that reason, He cannot be called anything except "One." He is properly one truth and one unity, and through His unity every single thing possesses its own unity. He is the first truth, nor does He require any other truth. For indeed, every thing receives its truth from Him; all things without Him...

<summary>This page opens the first book of the Picatrix with a metaphysical discourse, defining God as the "First Truth" and "Unity" from which all worldly knowledge and natural correspondences flow. It establishes knowledge as a divine gift that allows the practitioner to understand the hidden connections between all created things.</summary>

...imperfect. For He alone is perfect, and neither **Truth** nor **Unity** is perfect without Him. And through this it can be known what portion, and in what manner and how, any thing receives from Him, of which you may speak.

For He alone <note>original: "Ipse n: solus." "Nam" (for) is abbreviated here as "n:".</note> knows the rank and order of the generation and corruption of all **Creatures** <note>original: "Creaturarum." In this context, it refers to all created things in the universe, including plants, minerals, and animals, not just living beings.</note>; He knows which among them are last, which are first, and which are the middle cause of their corruption. He knows that these things themselves are not the cause of generation in any way, even though the middle things may contain a cause within their own corruption. And these things are the cause of corruption for all things existing beneath them.

The first of these is the cause of the generation and corruption of all other things existing beneath it; nothing exists that is higher or more perfect than it which could be the cause of its own generation or corruption. Nor is there anything besides it <gloss>the First Cause</gloss> that could perhaps know the order of created things—specifically <gloss>namely</gloss>, how and in what manner they are brought forth. Finally, [this is known] through the comparison of one thing to another, so that it may have a correspondence <note>original: "convenientiam." This refers to the "doctrine of signatures" or "sympathies," the idea that objects in the natural world are spiritually linked to one another and to the stars.</note> with the first things, and also how they descend through the order so that they have a correspondence with the last things. For He alone is the First, the perfect **Philosophy**, and the **Science of Truth**.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical introduction to the *Picatrix*, shifting from the nature of the First Cause (God) to the human pursuit of knowledge. And you should know that **knowledge** <term>knowledge: from the Latin *scire*, meaning the act of knowing or certain knowledge gained through study.</term> is a noble and supreme thing; and daily you ought to **study** <term>study: from *studere*, which in this context implies a devoted application of the mind, similar to "spiritual practice" or "diligent investigation."</term> in God and in His commandments and His goodness, because the knowledge of meaning and goodness proceeds from Him, and His Spirit is the noble and high light of the world. He who intends to study in Him ought to despise things of this sort <note>original: "Res huiusmodi." And you should know that God Himself is the maker and Creator of the whole world and of all things existing within it; and that the world itself, and all things existing in it, were created by the Most High Himself. And the reason for this is deep and powerful to comprehend—or at least that portion of it which can be comprehended through the study and knowledge of men. And this is the greatest gift that God gave to men: to study, to know, and to recognize. For to study is to serve God.

**Knowledge**, however, has three properties: 
1. The first is that it always acquires and never diminishes. 
2. The second is that it is always elevated and never lowered. <note>original: "diminuitur." The text uses the same verb as the first property, but in the context of "elevatur" (elevated), it likely means a loss of status or "being brought low."</note> 
3. The third is that it always appears and never hides itself. 

Likewise, knowledge has three strengths:
*   The first is that it makes one despise the things of this world.
*   The second is that it acquires good character.
*   The third is that it learns nothing except that which it loves within itself, and it impresses that upon the reason and the will.
