# SEVEN BOOKS BY THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSIUS:
## ON THE LORD’S SUPPER, TO CLEMENT
### THE SEVENTH ROMAN PONTIFF, In the Year 1530.

->Preface.<-

Not mine, but yours is the concern in this work I now labor upon regarding the Lord’s Supper, you Supreme Bishop and Prelate in every cathedral, to fall to your share, as you have set out to destroy the Temple of Christ. But you in Rome, who live in no small error, cause other errors to arise. For the decay of the Head <note>The "Head" refers to the Pope as the head of the Church.</note> is a cause of the straying of the members. Now, no member can be without a head; therefore, it is harmful that one Head gives rise to so many young heads.

St. Peter, your predecessor, conducted himself in such a way that no "purse-heads" <note>original: "haupt beutler." Likely a derogatory term for those focused on the church's finances or simony.</note> rose up or were awakened by him. It was perhaps a crude beginning, not according to your wisdom, but satiated with the Spirit, as befits a Head. Therefore, count yourself out from the number of those whom Christ announced and prophesied when He said that false prophets and false apostles shall arise. You shall consider your office and follow Christ our Savior; in doing so, you will first remove the beam from your own eye <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 7:5.</note>.

For you have the greatest lengths, and beneath them also the greatest splinters or shards. Therefore, the blind who station themselves before windows have small eyes, yet high and strong city walls. Thus, they have small loopholes in their eyes, yet they are like a Bishop. If you will now remove the filth from your eye, your influence will reach from the rising to the setting of the sun. Then you will remove the miserable sprouts <note>original: "Eldynen Sprießen." This refers to the offshoots or "suckers" growing from a tree, used here as a metaphor for ecclesiastical corruption.</note> that fall from your tree. But if you will not do this, the sprouts and chips will grow like a plane <note>original: "hobelgleich." This suggests the wood-shavings produced by a carpenter's plane, continuing the metaphor of the "beam" in the eye.</note>. Now, what profit is it for a man to be helped? How can you hope to be a shepherd of the sheep, as was commanded to Peter? They are not commanded to your state or your territory; nor were they commanded to the "Red Ones" <note>A reference to the Cardinals, known for their red vestments.</note> and those who wish to be shepherds. Therefore, because your blindness...

<meta>catchword: blindness.</meta>

<summary>This page serves as the preface to Paracelsus's 1530 treatise on the Eucharist, addressed to Pope Clement VII. Paracelsus delivers a scathing critique of the Papacy, accusing the Pope of corruption and spiritual blindness through vivid metaphors of wood, beams, and splinters.</summary>
<keywords>Paracelsus, Pope Clement VII, Lord's Supper, Reformation, St. Peter, Ecclesiastical Corruption, Biblical Metaphor, Papacy</keywords>

...blindness is punished, so open your eyes. Be enlightened in the Holy Spirit, so that you may step onto the Apostolic See <note>original: "Apostolischen Stuel." An archaic term for haughtiness or sinful pride.</note>: for there the hand is set. This is so that we may come into one sheepfold <note>original: "Schafftstall." A metaphor for the unified Church.</note>, and Christ be our Head, and the Spirit-Bishop remain established with Christ. In which sheepfold the Lord’s Supper of Christ <note>original: "Nachtmahl Christi"</note> shall be held according to the institution, as follows hereafter; this I wish to write to you above all others, for you to read further.

# The First Book

## Chapter 1.

As an introduction, it is to be understood in the Summary <note>original: "Summa." Refers here to the essential core or totality of the doctrine.</note> that there are two creatures <note>original: "Creaturn." In this context, it refers to two distinct "created natures" or entities within a single human being.</note> in man: the Divine and the Earthly. The Divine is created out of Adam through God the Father; the Earthly [is created] through God the Son, in everyone who believes in Him. <note>The text presents a striking reversal of traditional roles: here the "Divine" is linked to the original creation of Adam (the Father), while the "Earthly" (perhaps meaning the body renewed while on earth) is linked to the Son.</note> For whatever dies from the creation of God the Father does not rise again to Eternal Life, but [only] that which dies in God the Son. Therefore, the whole Summary consists in correctly recognizing these two creatures. These creatures have no substance and are nothing without material; they have resolved for themselves that nothing is dealt with for their body alone. 

Now, our body is only one body, namely [made] blessed of God the Father; and the creation of God the Son is added to it. And just as all the works of the Father are visible—the earth and everything—so the Son serves invisibly, and yet in both parts there is the same body, one form, shaped in everything by the power of God. 

Therefore, in the <term>Lord’s Supper</term> <note>original: "Cena Domini." The Latin term for the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, the intention is to correctly recognize these two bodies and their difference. And as the Father and Son are equal to one another, so also are we visible [as] the Father, and yet one Father. And visible [as] the Son, and yet one God. Thus we recognize the various works that remain in their form, but not [as] one body. God the Son does not create His creature differently than that of the Father, but He renews it; that is, He makes it like the other, and does not [re-]form it. For the old form remains standing in Heaven.

It does not pass through the old body. For it is indeed in the old body, but yet in the...

## CHAPTER IV.

The immortal body stands as indestructibly as the soul, for it possesses the nature and character of the soul and is always endowed with the same. Therefore, it passes through a wall just as Christ’s body passed through closed doors; for in this way the soul is united. The soul does not have a physical nature, but rather the opposite; yet they both possess a human nature. Therefore, this body goes to Him to whom it belongs: namely, to Christ. There it shall be fed alone, and shall not be consumed <note>original: "zehrend." Suggesting that unlike the mortal body which wastes away, this body is not subject to decay.</note> in the end. Therefore, we must not be distressed by sickness or desire to grasp or touch such a body [with mortal hands]; but always hold it as equal to the body of Christ, which went through closed doors, just as He rose through His divine power through the sealed tomb. That is the <term>Transfigured body (Verklärte leib): a body glorified by divine light, possessing supernatural properties while remaining human in form</term>, which is not subject to dead flesh.

The scripture of the prophets, as well as John the Evangelist <note>original: "Johā: Evangelista"</note>, concerns the Supper <note>original: "Nachtmal"</note>, which belongs here alongside the three Evangelists <note>Referring to the Synoptic Gospels: Matthew, Mark, and Luke</note>. Such things and others are not granted without the Holy Spirit. But no such person humbles himself. Their pride <term>Hoffart<explanation>An archaic German term for spiritual haughtiness or arrogance</explanation></term> is greater than the pride of the Emperor or the Turk; whereas if a man stood in such misery, he would become humble above all others. End of book 7 <note>original: "finis lib: 7."</note>.

# The Second Book
## from John the Evangelist <note>original Latin: "ex Johanne Euangelista"</note>

John Chapter 6 is to be held in particularly high regard as an explainer or interpreter of the other Evangelists, primarily regarding the sacramental power of the Lord's Supper <note>original: "Nachtmahl"</note> which the other three <note>Referring to the Synoptic Gospels: Matthew, Mark, and Luke</note> report; John explains all of that better and more fully than the other three. For he takes the explanation solely from the mouth of God, although he speaks somewhat more hiddenly or obscurely. Even though the other Evangelists also receive the Word of God and add nothing of their own or anything foreign to it, we must nevertheless grasp their meaning—or rather the Word of God—through the Holy Spirit, and not through the dead letter. And the sum of John's message is this: that salvation <note>original: "Seeligkeit"</note> must begin and exist within you. Whoever does not attain it during their lifetime will find it no more after their death. Therefore, those who are saved on earth must have their food of salvation on earth in the same way as it is in heaven, in the kingdom of the Father <note>original Latin: "in regno patris"</note>; and it is one single food. For there is one fellowship of the blessed in heaven and on earth, and not two different kinds. Therefore, one food has been ordained by Christ: for His will is in heaven as it is on earth. Accordingly, whoever does not eat here on earth from the table of Christ is also deprived of it in heaven. Therefore, John stands upon this foundation—namely, in the interpretation of the power of this food, which is eternal life <note>original Latin: "Vita aeterna"</note>, not in the order of the flesh <note>original Latin: "carnis"</note>. For he says:

> Work for the food that remains <note>original Latin: "Operamini Cibum qui manet," quoting John 6:27</note>

From this, it is well to be understood that this food is no mere filling of the belly, but rather an imperishable and abiding food for our eternal life; for this is the fundamental meaning of that passage.

> Which the Son of Man will give <note>original Latin: "Quem filius hominis dabit"</note>

That is Christ, the Son of Man: therefore He gives you the food, as a man, to eat bodily—not as a ghost or a shadow—but yet it is spiritual, heavenly, and eternal food, which death cannot grasp in eternity.

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the Eucharist (the Lord's Supper) and the nature of Christ's presence. The previous page emphasized that spiritual understanding requires the Father’s guidance and that Christ must be seen not through the lens of fallen human nature ("Adam’s flesh"), but through the "New Birth." This page specifically addresses the relationship between the physical elements of bread and wine and the spiritual reality of Christ’s flesh and blood.</meta>

The bread of the Lord's Supper and the flesh of Christ must not be separated from one another. For where one is received, the other is also understood to be present; but where they are separated in their use <note>The "use" refers to the ritual practice of the sacrament.</note>, confusion follows. Thus, one must not eat the natural flesh of Christ in the manner in which He died on the tree <note>The "tree" refers to the Cross.</note>. That was never Christ’s intention; therefore, He meant the presence of His flesh to be with the bread, and not without the bread.

Christ would not have let the eating of the bread stop at the teeth, but added: **My words are spirit and they are life** <note>original: "Verba mea spiritus sunt, et vita sunt" — a reference to John 6:63.</note>. By this, we take it through the mouth <note>original: "per os"</note>, but not into the stomach. We must also, in the same way, [receive] the blood that flows from the flesh. Therefore, the outcome would have no meaning without the Word; because since His command is there, it must be testified in the Supper and believed: that it is the work [of atonement] for our sin to eat and taste the flesh and the blood of Christ.

For how else would it be possible for us, by our own strength and without the Supper, to follow Christ’s command in bare faith? Just as we are physically redeemed by Christ, so we must also be physically fed by Him! For His body is our redemption; therefore His flesh is also our food, and not in bare faith alone. Therefore He says further: **My flesh is truly food** <note>original: "Caro mea vere est cibus" — a reference to John 6:55.</note>.

For our flesh of the new birth <term>rebirth/new creation: the spiritual transformation of a person through Christ</term>, or the [newly created] creature, must have flesh, and not bare spirit. Therefore, the one must not be divided from the other; thus the works of faith or the Spirit are in the Body, and vice versa <note>original: "et contra"</note>. It is not human flesh that is our food, nor human blood that is our drink; rather, the bread and wine are our food and drink, which is called the flesh and blood of Christ. And it is the same in a hidden form: just as a human is composed of a soul, and the soul is within him, so it is in the rebirth from Christ—He remains in us.

<meta>This page continues the theological commentary from the previous page, moving from Peter's confession of faith in John 6 to a broader interpretation of the "Word" as spiritual bread. # The Third Book
## Being an interpretation of several sayings found throughout the four Evangelists pertaining to the Lord’s Supper. <note>original: "nachmal" – likely a variant of "Nachtmahl," referring to the Holy Supper or Eucharist.</note>

Because the text in the Gospel books is, by its very nature, always rejected by human reason in the same manner, it is no wonder that the sayings regarding the main articles of faith are so strangely altered by people. For in the main point, or the "chief piece," the one who feels <note>or "the perceiver"</note> fails in many sayings in those matters that are not aligned with the [sacramental] elements. This happens because they place reason above the ordinances of God. Nevertheless, Christ did not only have humans as adversaries, but also the Devil, and the Devil had his own knights <note>original: "ritter"</note> on his side who set themselves against Christ. And these spirits have a greater understanding than humans. But when humans let themselves be deceived by such spirits and devils, that is their great unbelief. And it is a great mercy for us that He allowed Himself to enter into the persistence of damnation <note>This likely refers to Christ’s descent or His taking on the human condition of those condemned to death.</note>. Therefore, Christ encountered many things. Because of this, He had to make Himself heard and understood in many ways through words that might be interpreted against Him then and His words thereafter.

In the same way, the Devil also tempted Christ and desired much from him, such as: "make bread from these stones" <note>original Latin: "vt: fac i lapidib panem"</note>. Not because he wanted to be the master here, but rather because he wanted to enter into a fellowship <note>original: "jnfren schaft," likely "Infraschaft" or "Gefährtenschaft" meaning companionship or alliance.</note> with Him. People of his kind do the same to Him.

Man lives by two kinds of bread: the earthly-Adamic and the Heavenly. The heavenly bread is the eternal **Word of God’s proclaimer** <term>Verbum predicatoris Dei <note>the Word as preached or proclaimed by God</note></term>: namely, the Word of God that comes out of the mouth of God. For the Word, which became flesh—**JESUS CHRIST**—means that man shall consist of two kinds of bread. That is: not the eternal man alone (namely the Adamic, old, earthly one), but the New Man as well; and a King; and two breads and one Man are also present here.

The Devil did not understand this word of Christ. Christ answered the Devil humanly according to his demand and the question, but He did not answer from the Devil’s heart. For the Devil desired in his heart to know the heavenly bread and questioned the Lord about it. Now, the **Bread of the flesh** <term>Caro panis</term> will not be useful as flesh alone, but rather the **Flesh of the Word in the resurrection** <term>Caro verbi in resurrectione</term>. For the flesh of Adam is, in and of itself, worth nothing at all, because it is without spirit and dead.

...and is life, for the spirit is our life. And Christ is the flesh and blood born of the Holy Virgin Mary, who has come down from above. Thus, the **New Creature** <note>A reference to the "new creation" in 2 Corinthians 5:17, meaning the person spiritually reborn in Christ.</note> stands within the old. Likewise, the flesh of Christ and His blood are of no use without His spirit. Judas ate the flesh of Christ and drank His blood without His spirit; therefore, it was of no benefit to him. Now, the **Gospel** <note>original: "Evangelium."</note> is the Word of God. Thus, man lives by the Gospel; that is, he lives by every word of God that proceeds through the mouth of God. Therefore, let no one here misunderstand "all words of God," for all words of God are the Gospel. The Gospel is the voice of God—as it is written in the 94th Psalm, verse 8: "Today, if you hear my voice" <note>original Latin: "Hodie n[enim]: si Vocem meam audieritis." In most modern Bibles, this is Psalm 95:7-8.</note>. The voice of God is the voice of God the Father and God the Son; it is one voice, and that [voice] is the **Holy Spirit**. And it cannot be separated from the body of God, just as the body of God cannot exist without the Holy Spirit. Thus, we live by the Bread and with the Gospel, which is an image of both body and spirit. Therefore, we eat for the sake of eternal life, and in eating, we also pray that we may receive it. For to [reject this] is the sin against the Holy Spirit, which will be forgiven neither in heaven nor on earth.

These Christians or saints (beloved through the grace of God’s Word) should despise no nation. Rather, fellowship is the unceasing cause [of their life], so that they [learn] from us what is useless or brings suffering, and not from those [nations]. <note>This suggests that Christians should serve as examples to others rather than holding them in contempt.</note> Christ acted in this way with the **heathen woman** <note>original: "Heijdenweiblin," referring to the Canaanite or Syrophoenician woman (Matthew 15:21–28) who demonstrated great faith despite being a Gentile.</note>. For we should give to the unbelievers and instruct them firmly; if they do not [listen], then we are excused, for we have done what is required of us as Christians.

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of Christ's physical and spiritual presence, moving from the discussion of "spiritual bread" on the previous page to the "living water" encountered in the Gospel of John. The author is drawing a parallel between the water offered to the Samaritan woman and the blood of Christ, emphasizing that spiritual reality often hides behind earthly forms.</meta>

The water Christ spoke about and gave to the **Samaritan woman** <note>original: "Samritisch weib"; a reference to the encounter at the well in John 4.</note> in **John 4** is nothing other than His blood.

Now notice here that Christ may call His blood whatever He wishes, because Christ gives His blood from time to time as He wills—not appearing as blood, but in an earthly form. Who would want to be contentious about this, even if He said, "The water that I give you is my blood just as much as the wine is"? We are able to drink Christ's blood in a way that those [without faith] cannot. And if this young woman had desired or understood it, He would have answered her with His blood in the form of water, and would have called it the **living water**. Such a thing requires nothing else; for Christ seeks no pride in eating. And although the young woman did not understand the Lord Christ’s voice, she nevertheless powerfully enjoyed the fruit of His meaning.

He can give His blood to be drunk in water if He pleases, for there is no lack or defect in Him who created water. Learn also to understand the Gospel of John best: that although our eyes see only water, it is not merely water, but rather **water springing up into eternal life** <note>original Latin: "aqua salientes in vitam aeternam"; quoting John 4:14.</note>. By this, Christ powerfully gives us to understand and confirms that our water, when mixed [in the liturgy], does not fall outside His history. # The Fourth Book from St. Paul

<margin>Paul</margin>
If there were a different nature to the Lord's Supper than what the Evangelists <note>The authors of the Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.</note> demonstrate, then Paul would not have described it [as he did]. However, he lets it remain as the Evangelists have it, without any figures of speech or tropes <term>tropus: a figurative or metaphorical use of a word</term>, so that it remains truly eating and drinking. It is true, but not "natural" (in the sense of how nature works), for what is natural passes through the stomach or the body. This other [eating] does not. Otherwise, one thing follows: therefore it remains and increases.

Paul is the interpreter <note>original: "interpres"</note> or the messenger <note>original: "Hermet:" likely referring to Hermes, the Greek messenger of the gods</note> of Christ: and through him all our disputes are handled (primarily in the controversy regarding the Lord's Supper), and through his sufficiency, some doubts are set aside.

Because Paul leaves a human body in the Lord's Supper—which a person simply understands and grasps, even as our language allows—we should also let it remain at that. We should not pull any angelic <note>original: "Englyschen," likely meaning "angelic" (high-spiritual) rather than the nationality</note> supernatural understanding into it, nor make spiritual that which Christ intended physically. And in that way—eating and drinking the body and blood of Christ—we should understand it as the words sound. But as to how it happens, we cannot grasp that with our reason. Because the shell <note>The outward physical elements of bread and wine.</note> is included, we must be taught from above and be reborn. We do not grasp it otherwise than through faith and trust in Christ: that it is what He said it was, even if we see something else with our eyes. This occurs through the power of the words of the Supper. Then, if we come into ourselves: we cannot grasp ourselves better than here, so that we are in his attached humanity; it is there that we eat the words: and [find] peace against unbelief.

Contradictory things are given from the cloisters <note>A reference to monastic or Roman Catholic teachings that the author finds problematic.</note> regarding the bread and wine. For our eyes see nothing but failing things. Therefore, in nature, we must nonetheless comply with God’s command, which is: Eat and Drink. We wish to preserve our bodies for the hereafter, God granting it how He will: whether we understand how the power flows into us or not. Thus, the more we receive the flesh and blood of Christ, the more we wish to live in the Spirit. Therefore, how much more must we believe and trust in Christ, since we trust His Father. Therefore, the human is commanded [to partake] in both creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to the created elements of the sacrament.</note>, wine and bread <note>original: "Votrā," likely a transcription error or abbreviation for "Brot" (bread)</note>; the Spirit follows the human way through these deeds, and we enjoy and understand it. For from Paul it is clearly to be seen that the word of God and His body are not two bodies, but one. God the Father created man through His word: Now He has not taken the word from him, but left it with him. That is now the life that the human has. Therefore...

Paul does not give the authority to eat and drink; rather, God the Father has given the authority to eat and drink those foods whenever we wish. And just as we do not ask where earthly food comes from, but simply remember the fullness of the earth—namely, that it belongs to the Lord—so too is the food of Christ to be understood. We should follow its course and not torment our consciences with questions; rather, remember that the Lord is all fullness, grace upon grace, righteousness, power, and might.

But now, after his death, he gives himself to us physically in his life, yet invisibly in the food here. Therefore, for the sake of the eyes alone, it might be called "spiritual," but this is inaccurate <note>original Latin: *improprie*</note>; for the sake of the heirs, it is not spiritual [in the sense of being non-physical] at all. ## Flee from the Worship of Idols <note>original Latin: "Fugite simulachrorū Cultus."</note>

From these words, a clear departure is to be noted from the Mass and "idol-works," in which the Lord's Supper would be defiled. Therefore, one should in no way stand by the Mass. For if we consider what the Mass is with all its decoration, it is fundamentally nothing but "idol-work" or [human] labor. Now see with what great reverence Paul the Apostle commands the Supper to us: that we should now be wise and understanding, and not place our fleshly selves again—or outside of Him (who has made us entirely clean)—under the idols. We should not become strangers to the Testament, but rather persevere in the Lord and not with idols; keeping watch with our heart as His temple, secure in His remembrance. And even if false prophets persuade us, God gives us everything so that we may confess Him.

Therefore, we should prepare ourselves with real earnestness for His Supper without idolatry. How could those people reconcile <note>original: "bereimen," literally to rhyme or make sense of.</note> the right contemplation and the healthy use and memory of the Lord’s suffering, who are there playing organs and singing, or who so easily "swarm" <note>A reference to the "Swermer" or fanatics mentioned earlier.</note>? In that Mass, they sing and dance where they should more rightly weep and wail over the great sins with which they brought Him, their Savior, into such suffering and death, anxiety and need.

It is pitiable; Paul not unjustly notes and addresses those supposed heretics, as he indicated to them. He asks that we should flee such things, we who eat as many from one bread as one body.

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the Lord's Supper, contrasting the communal meal of Christ with the "idolatrous" practices of the Catholic Mass and pagan rituals. The author uses St. Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians (specifically chapters 10 and 11) to argue that the Eucharist is a meal to be eaten for spiritual nourishment, not a sacrifice to be performed by a priest.</meta>

From this, it follows that everyone who eats of the bread and the body of Christ is himself a priest in Christ, without any idolatry; however, this is only with the heart and the memory of His life, received and shared through the mouth. And just as those who eat the [ancient] sacrifices become partakers of the sacrifice, so also do we who partake of the unique sacrifice of Christ—that is, His body and blood. Because of this, we shall rise again to eternal praise.

### What do I say regarding idols? <note>original Latin: "Quid dico quod simulacris?" A reference to 1 Corinthians 10:19, where Paul asks if an idol or food offered to idols has any power.</note>

Do I wish, unfortunately, for the heathen sacrifices to be understood [as having power]? We are meant to eat the bread [of the Lord], but not according to heathen customs, which have no right to eat it. By this, we understand that their [idolatrous] service is nothing. We must in no way allow heathen or strange customs to persist. For in the New Testament, all <note>original: "simulachra"</note> idols are abolished. Therefore, we should not offer sacrifices, for our priest [Christ] was not given to be sacrificed [repeatedly], but to be eaten and drunk, and also to let us become partakers of the Temple, which is Christ.

### The Cup of the Lord, etc. <note>original Latin: "Poculum Domini etc." Refers to 1 Corinthians 10:21: "You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons."</note>

We cannot serve two masters; therefore, we cannot have two orders [of worship], but only one alone, and that is the Lord’s. Because of this, we should examine ourselves well beforehand, so that we do not eat and drink damnation, and do not eat the Devil’s supper or enjoy their tables. It was not in vain that St. Paul reported this. For the table of the Lord Christ is the Lord’s own ordinance, just as He gave us an example.

<margin>The idolatrous one is the altar of idols that attempts to step into Christian decoration. Therefore, one table must yield to the other.</margin>

Therefore, we desire to be the Lord’s table; since we flee the Devil’s table, the heart alone will henceforth be our table. For two contradictory things cannot exist together, such as the table of <term>Mammon</term> <note>original: "Messmon." A biblical term for wealth or greed personified as a false god. The author suggests one cannot feast on worldly/idolatrous things while feasting on Christ.</note> drunk with the table of Christ. For He certainly would not suffer us to defy Him and try to unite Him with the Devil. Rather, we should seek Him alone, for our constancy and benefit. Christ is our benefit and salvation, whereas we ourselves are otherwise nothing.

### There must be factions among you <note>original Latin: "Oportet sectas inter vos esse." A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:19.</note>

Many are called, but few are chosen. Now, it was not right to call only the chosen. Paul sets down the reason for this: namely, so that those who are righteous may be recognized from those who are not chosen. For those who are not out... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

# The Fifth Book from the
## Prophecy of the Prophets

<margin>
As was mentioned at the beginning, all points and articles of the Christian faith, as they are contained in the Gospel, cannot be thoroughly known or understood apart from the writings of the prophets. Therefore, as far as the prophets indicate, we should administer our faith, and so forth.
</margin>

As was mentioned at the beginning, all points and articles of the Christian faith, as they are contained in the Gospel, cannot be thoroughly known or understood apart from the writings of the prophets. Therefore, as far as the prophets indicate, we should administer our faith, and so forth.

Now, concerning the <term>Supper</term> <note>original: "Nachtmal," literally "night-meal," referring to the Eucharist or Lord's Supper</note>, it is the highest article among all others of faith in Christ; therefore, we should rightly and diligently look through the prophets so that we do not go astray in this article. For here lies the acceptable sacrifice of the <term>New Creature</term> <note>A common Reformation-era term for the believer who has been spiritually reborn or "regenerated" in Christ</note>, in which all law was fulfilled. Therefore, we must believe everything that Christ says, that it is so; and within that faith, hide a simple eating and drinking, and bodily enjoy that which the teeth cannot grasp.

Now, it is conceivable that two kinds of eating are understood: one bodily and one spiritual. And also, each person may <unclear>s</unclear> believe <unclear>s</unclear> it will be so; however, it is not to be taken that way. For the Spirit of the Lord and Christ are not separated from one another. Therefore, it cannot be eaten spiritually here unless it is also bodily, *and vice versa* <note>original Latin: "et contra"</note>.

In the Supper, nothing can be eaten [merely] spiritually. For the Spirit offered itself in death, or was hanged, and became flesh in our Lady Mary. Where are Spirit and Flesh [separated] from one another, *and vice-versa*? Therefore, whoever wishes to have one must also have the other. For the sake of our flesh, the bare flesh is of no use; but that which is God-enlivened by the Spirit, united with the flesh, is useful. And if Christ’s flesh is to be rightly named, it is a spiritual flesh or a spiritualized flesh. For that is what the Spirit has "spirited" <note>original: "gegeistet," a mystical term implying the Spirit has permeated or transformed the matter</note>, which is conceived by the Spirit and not by man. God is the Word that became flesh and what the flesh <unclear>has</unclear>

> Paul says: The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, a central text for those arguing for a spiritual rather than literal interpretation of scripture and sacraments</note>

The letter is from the letter, the letter; therefore it is dead. But the Spirit is from the understanding, and is God Himself. If, then, the letter is not of God, is it then of any use to you? Therefore, the letter must be of God. For this reason, Christ’s flesh did not grow from the earth, though it truly was flesh and looked like other flesh according to nature.

The prophets have prepared us with their interpretation from the Holy Spirit, just as they did for the ancient Jews, as things that signify at hand, or the maintenance of such a being: thus it was prophesied of Him. But the Spirit of Christ interprets everything so that the Word of Christ is rightly understood and preached. Thus, no forerunner of the Word of God should <unclear>s s</unclear> <unclear>be-</unclear> draw up the word [except] from the Holy Spirit. For they, the prophets, prepare [the way]. The prophets are everything to us according to God’s law. Therefore, if the prophet does not [dwell] in them, but the whole sum of the Holy Gospel [does], then that proclamation is not dismayed. For such people only make a mockery, who think of the temple of God and trust the universal Church of God. For they are also born from above out of God.

V. 11.</margin> where he says: "Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it." <note>original: "Dilata os tuum, & implebo illud"; this is actually Psalm 81:10 in modern numbering.</note> Therefore Asaph teaches very strongly throughout the whole psalm, and gives us to understand repentance in the first verses, which we do not observe as diligently following after this day of Solemnity. There is no other day than the day of the Lord's Supper <note>original: "Cena Domini"</note>. For on that day is our highest joy and greatest wedding feast, when Christ speaks with his disciples, saying: "This is my body."

<margin>V. 2.</margin> "Great are the works of the Lord, and sought out according to all his desires." <note>original: "Magna opera Domini, & exquisita in omnes voluntates eius" (Psalm 111:2)</note> Therefore, God wants His great works of the Supper to be known and understood. <margin>V. 3.</margin> "His splendor and his righteousness." <note>original: "Magnificentia eius & iustitia eius" (Psalm 111:3)</note> Just as his confession proceeds from the heart—love and faithfulness—so also the Word was spoken by Christ when he said: "This is my body." Who will speak against this righteousness...

<margin>V. 4.</margin> "He has made a memorial of his wonders." <note>original: "Memoriam fecit mirabilium suorum" (Psalm 111:4)</note> In these verses is the sum and the foundation of the whole psalm, which also consoles the work of the Supper; for this is the wonder he performed with his own, and created a new world for them.

Through this, Christ has bound himself to us. He has done it in such a way that whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood—while keeping the Articles of Faith in mind as a memorial of him—remains truly in Christ and a Christian believer.

**"That he may give them the power of the inheritance of the Gentiles"** <note>original: "Virtutem ut det illis hereditatem Gentium" from Psalm 111:6</note>: Christ's body becomes <unclear>present</unclear> <note>The Latin abbreviation "pntialis" likely refers to "praesentialis" or presential, meaning the real presence of Christ.</note> as a friend's, yet a prisoner to an enemy; however, he is never the loser. <meta>This page transitions from a specific theological discussion of the Eucharist in the Psalms to a broader philosophical exploration of the "Light of Nature." It establishes the relationship between natural wonders and divine revelation, arguing that the mysteries of nature serve as parables for spiritual truths.</meta>

# The Sixth Book on the Light
-> of Nature. <-

There are two kinds of arts: those of Nature, and those received in the Holy Spirit. Those who praise the Spirit do not disparage the service of Nature. Others, who do not live in the Holy Spirit, are already grounded in Nature. For these same unbelievers, God has set forth such wonderful miraculous works so that even if someone were ever so hardened in unbelief, he might still be moved to faith by these works. For the higher an unbeliever is grounded in the Light of Nature, the higher he is experienced in the miraculous works of God; thus, an eternal, irrefutable God must be recognized through His works. As Christ therefore also says: "If you will not believe me, then believe my works." <note>A reference to John 10:38.</note> For this reason, Christ also gave many parables <note>original: "Parabelas"</note> from the Light of Nature. Therefore, one should recognize the mysteries <note>original: "misteria"</note> of Nature well, so that these parables may be all the better understood. For this reason, Christ did not act contrary to Nature, but rather fulfilled its works; what Nature works through its course, the Lord Christ worked through His word. Thus, medicine <note>original: "medicina"</note> makes one healthy through the powers of Nature—now here come the internal drivers <note>referring to internal biological or spiritual forces</note> which are ours. Christ, however, makes one healthy simply <note>original: "simpliciter"</note> through the word. For it is He of whom Sirach says in the 38th Chapter that He lets medicine grow out of the earth; <note>referring to Sirach 38:4: "The Lord created medicines out of the earth, and a sensible man will not despise them."</note> He is the one who creates medicine, or the Creator of medicine, and therefore also the highest Physician, for in Him is the highest essence of the Light of Nature. Therefore, in this book, two kinds of parables are discussed. Some parables move clever people who, through their understanding, also draw meaning into parables. Secondly, there are the "Great Deeds" <term>Magnalia</term> <note>refers to the great works of God in the physical world</note> and the "Secrets of Nature" <term>Arcana Natura</term>, which lead to such an introduction of parables themselves. For these great deeds have been prophecies lying from the beginning of the world until the coming of Christ their Creator, and they bear witness until the end of the world.

Doves <term>that is, Columbæ</term> <note>Latin for doves</note> are entirely without care; they build no concern for their food and worry nothing about the winter, but rather trust in luck.

Snakes have their great foresight in the open: they bite their own medicine <note>likely a reference to the folk belief that snakes know herbs for self-healing</note>; they make stones for themselves against various accidents, and they cover themselves with various improvements of natural knowledge.

Ravenous wolves <term>Lupi rapaces</term> <note>Latin for "predatory wolves"</note>: the wolf’s nature is envious of mankind; it presses upon and touches a person however it can.

So also is the nature of the sheep, which may feed upon what a person provides and knows from him what it can. Now, the wolf and the sheep are not a powerful parable with each other or together, for they are of one nature, even if they are not of one being.

But bread cannot be a parable of Christ’s suffering, because it has neither His nature nor His property, nor can it ever be <unclear>judged</unclear> by the way of Nature. The Paschal Lamb would indeed have been a parable of Him, if you had honored it as such.

The Lamb of God <term>Agnus Dei</term> is a correct parable, not for the sake of its form, but for its nature. For God gave the lamb—and therefore His Son had to be the Lamb—a strong heart and a living property.

But this is not to be understood in the same way with the bread.

**The Light of the World** <note>original: "Lux Mundi"</note>; for just as light is a guide for mankind, so too are the Apostles "lights"—guides for human souls. **Salt of the Earth** <note>original: "Sal terrae"</note>; What food is good without salt? In the same way, what man is good without the Spirit? The right diligence belongs to the Apostles today. The Apostles make us ready for holiness. For their teaching and example do not deceive; otherwise, God Himself, through them, [would be] the flesh of the earth that is evil; but He takes nothing through the Apostles [that is not transformed]. Salt is in all the world; so must the Apostles be received. Salt preserves against rot; thus, one is preserved <note>original: "Balsamiert," literally "embalmed" or "treated with balsam"</note> **unto eternal life** <note>original: "ad Vitam aeternā"</note>, just as all raw flesh is **preserved** <note>original: "conserviert"</note> by the **properties** <note>original: "proprietatibüs"</note> of the spirit of salt. The Apostles are not salt themselves, but their teaching is like salt.

But bread and Christ cannot be joined together either **in expression** <note>original: "in dictione"</note> nor in **meaning** <note>original: "sententia"</note>, neither by nature nor by quality—**that is, by their properties** <note>original: "h. e. proprietatibüs"</note>. Christ did not say: "My Body," or "**this body is my Body**" <note>original: "hoc corpus est Corpus meum"</note>. That would be a mere comparison. **"I am the Vine"** <note>original: "Ego sū Vitis"</note>: Earlier He had not said, "I am the bread." To hold it in one's hands and have it be a comparison. Rather, He is the **True Vine** <note>original: "Vitis Vera"</note>. This is also a true comparison. For just as the grapevine is pleasant to all people and is the refreshment of love and community among all people: so also should the great love and hope be in Christ. And His blood must be better than all wine. Therefore, it is a true comparison, through which we may recognize the use of His blood. Thus, the parables are of one mind, and so are we who hold to this understanding. Therefore, all **figurative usages** <note>original: "Tropisein," referring to the use of rhetorical tropes or metaphors</note> arise from human understanding and remain within the same.

But Christ, in the words of the Last Supper, did not establish the <unclear>nature</unclear> of human nature; rather, He established faith, love, and the bitter death of His holy **Covenant of the Testament** <note>original: "Testamentbündniß"</note> and remembrance. For that reason, He did not use any "Light of Nature" in a merely human way there. How then can earthly man establish—**that is** <note>original: "h. e."</note>—that our comparison should be between that which is from above and that which is from below <unclear>Heaven</unclear>? **That is**: human understanding compared with the Divine word.

What follows is the preaching and prophecy according to the content of the Gospels of God. The **Wisdom** <note>original: "Magia," here likely referring to spiritual wisdom or the "magical" power of the Word</note> which no flesh could possess. For the prophets proclaim future things concerning the Son of God. Just as the prophets prophesied skillfully above nature concerning the course of nature and the influence of the heavens, so also the Gospels do not have their "taste" from the nature of the heavenly influence. Rather, they are the truths of God. And all other things are otherwise; He touches His <unclear>mystic-train</unclear>. Thus, they are also inwardly possessed by this quiet contemplation. Therefore, whoever will not believe the word of God...

...of God, yet believes in His works. Also, so that no one may excuse themselves [by claiming] they did not understand or grasp it. Therefore, God has placed [these signs] before our eyes for the benefit of our reason. But the faithful do not need them, for they have enough in the Word.

The Virgin with the water in the sieve, which remained therein, signifies the birth of Christ from a Virgin. <note>This refers to the classical legend of the Vestal Virgin Tuccia, who proved her purity by carrying water in a sieve without spilling a drop. <margin>PHOENIX</margin> The phoenix has such a <term>great wonder</term> <note>original: "magnalia"; refers to the inherent miraculous powers God placed in nature</note> within it: when its old age begins to weigh upon it, it gathers dry wood together and makes a hollow place for itself in the center. Then it flies higher than all other birds and shoots down like a lightning bolt into the wood, igniting it all around. This signifies that we are nothing from our mother's womb; therefore, we must be rightly formed by the One and by God with all His power. Likewise, it is a prophecy of the New Birth: that we must be recast into a new form, otherwise there would be nothing good in us.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how natural phenomena serve as "signs" for divine truths. While the previous page used animal metaphors (the phoenix) to explain rebirth, this page uses the "Light of Nature" and the process of digestion to explain the Eucharist and the nature of "flesh and blood."</meta>

Therefore, in the light of nature, it is found that not all things are what we perceive them to be: for our eye always perceives only the outward appearance of **bodies**. <note>original: "Corporum"; in this context, it refers to the physical, material substance as opposed to its spiritual or "potential" essence.</note> Thus, everything we eat and drink is actually flesh and blood, but we do not see it as such. For this reason, we should not always trust our sight; for example, we look at wheat and see only grain, yet it is nonetheless flesh and blood. It may be ox flesh or green flesh, but not yet human: however, when it is eaten by a human, it is transformed within that body into human flesh and blood. Thus, all legumes and other things that serve as food are <term>potential human flesh in a mystery</term>. <note>The author is using a proto-biochemical argument: food has the "potential" (potentia) to become human tissue through the "mystery" of digestion.</note> Likewise, concerning wine and drink, we find in the Scriptures the phrase "drunken blood"; this is all spoken in reference to the final matter. <note>original: "materia"; the end state of a substance after it has been processed or "perfected."</note>

In the same way: all things come from the fruit of the earth and take their **body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note> from it. Now, the fruit of the earth comes from above, and the earth provides the body: so we humans are nothing without that same fruit which sustains us, but that fruit transforms entirely into our flesh and blood, since it originates as the fruit of the earth.

For at the beginning, when we are conceived and born, we are neither blood nor flesh, because in the mother’s womb there is neither [finished] flesh nor blood: from that conception, the human body receives only its form from the seed. When we are born, the mother’s milk is our food and drink, [derived] from her blood and flesh: and it becomes everything that is within us. But once we outgrow the milk, we are strengthened in our body like a tree that draws the sap of the earth; we are sustained by food, which is the movement of the **great world into the small**. <note>This refers to the "Macrocosm" (the universe/earth) entering the "Microcosm" (the human being). In Paracelsian thought, man contains the entire world within himself.</note> For all other things serving as food and drink are nothing other than the body of man.

Therefore, no one should wonder how bread and wine can be the body and blood of Christ. Since it is said here that every food and drink becomes the blood of our body, anyone can say of any food or drink: "This is my body and blood," once it is eaten by us.

<margin>of God</margin>
This is now manifest, despite your lies. For it is found to be so naturally, even if it does not appear so clearly to our eyes. For God the Father wished to feed our body with invisible bodies in many various forms, yet it becomes pure within our stomach.

Thus, Christ—who is a man—could also point to bread and wine and say that it is His body and blood; for He certainly possessed a human body and blood, just like other men. <term>Mark this example</term>. I suppose that I had my nourishment, according to my necessity, in daily ordered food and drink as a single meal [destined] to become my flesh and blood. Now, by chance, a hungry and thirsty man comes to me. And I give him, before I myself can eat, half of my daily necessity. Could I not say: "He eats my body and drinks my blood"? For I give him so much of my substance, that is: from my own body, and not from the substance of other people, but from my own food and portion.

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of substance and the body. While the previous page discussed how natural food becomes human flesh through a "mystery" of transformation, this page applies that logic to Christ’s Supper (the Eucharist) and the creation of the "New Creature" through the Holy Spirit.</meta>

...simple folk might be won over, so that they might better grasp Christ’s Supper.

<margin>a</margin>
Might it not be sufficient, or already answered before God or Jesus, according to the Father in His act of creating?

Now, the disciples of Christ at the Supper might have said to their Master: "Lord, the bread that you give us is also **my** body, and not your body alone." To this, let the following example serve as an answer (as previously stated regarding the *movable giving of the actual substance*): The bread that Christ took into His hand was His natural, unmixed **outward substance** <note>original: "Ob[er]"; likely short for *Oberfläche* (surface/outward appearance) or *Objekt*. The author is distinguishing between the physical bread and its spiritual potential.</note> according to bodily appearance and form. Now, however, He broke it and gave it from Himself; therefore, the disciples might well have rightly asked, "In what manner have we eaten your body?"

And when Christ says, "That which is given for you," it is understood that because He offered His body, the body is called such in the very substance of that which He gives. In this way, Christ’s flesh is often **set aside** <note>original: "frustrert"; in this context, it suggests that the physical, carnal understanding of flesh is frustrated or bypassed.</note> until we come into His Kingdom. This is brought about by the union and thanksgiving, upon which faith is set, just as upon a firm **foundation** <note>original: "baten"; likely *Boden* (ground/soil).</note> of His word.

For what is miraculously made out of things wherein neither reason nor wisdom weighed; and in this earth, it was neither light nor flesh. But from the word of God, man became flesh and blood. In his dwelling, he was created far from God. Now, it is a great thing before His power that the man of the creation became flesh and blood. But in the **endowment of Mary** <note>The Incarnation; the process by which Christ took on human form through the Virgin Mary.</note>, all His food and drink became His flesh and blood. Thus is man a Son of God, for He has no other Father. May not God the Father then say: "That human child is mine, for I have indeed made everything in him. For everything that man has is mine. And when he eats, it is my flesh and blood. Thus he remains in me, and I in him: And I am his condemnation and salvation."

Through this I now ask: Is not Christ’s power also thus? Has He not been commanded to create the **New Creature**? <term>New Creature</term> <note>original: "Neue Creatur"; a theological concept referring to a person who has been spiritually reborn or "re-created" through Christ.</note> May He not also say to our faith, and by the power of His divinity and His creation: "This is my body, and you are my body and blood"? Thus does God the Father **propagate** <note>original: "propagat"; to reproduce or continue the lineage of the "Old Creature" (Adam).</note> the old creation. And just as we are born anew from above, and receive from the Holy Spirit through Christ, and die in the body of Adam: so is the drink of Christ received from above from the Holy Spirit, and the flesh taken from Mary. That same body died on the cross; and that same blood was shed for our sake. Therefore Christ gives the same...

# Book VII.
## On the Worthy Use of the Lord's Supper.

In order that we may celebrate the Lord's Supper worthily, the teaching of Paul to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 10:17ff and following) must be well understood. For we have here before us not a mere symbol, but the true flesh and blood of Christ, through which we are either glorified or condemned. Therefore, we must take up two things:
1. That we cleanse the **Lord's Supper** <note>original: "Cœnam Domini"</note> from all kinds of idolatry. 2. That we understand the true foundation of why we enjoy the Lord's Supper of Christ.
The first part does away with ceremonies and idolatrous teachings. 2. It teaches against the additions and the alteration of the [original] Order. For the memory [of Christ] remains through its [proper] use, not in alterations and additions. 
Therefore, it should not happen in any temple <note>The author refers to traditional, ornate church buildings as "temples" to contrast them with the simpler "houses" of the early church.</note>. For it is there that idolatries are made. The Altar is a piece of idolatry. <margin>the garments etc.</margin> As long as these things are displayed and used, it is a contempt for the Suffering of Christ. Likewise, all idolatrous clothing and vestments should be done away with. We should also flee the [ritual] actions and voices of such persons.

Secondly, the proclamation should happen in this way: that we go and confess to the unbelievers and proclaim His death. Among the believers, this is not necessary. For those who believe in the death of Christ also believe everything else.
Now, note an explanation concerning these two points. The idolatrous crowds heap up a <term>Sacrament</term> <note>Referring here to the physical host or the ritual act of the Mass.</note> upon which they give it; they proclaim the death of Christ without fruit. The heart is far from the mouth, and in their hearts and their intentions, it is a dead proclamation from which no fruit grows.
The true memory lies in the heart, and the true proclamation in the mouth. The power of the heart is love in Christ. But the love of the heart drives the tongue to proclaim the death of the Lord Christ to the unbelievers. Now, in times of need, friends are tested. <margin>the right way is worth nothing to the idolatrous company. Compare it to the Apostles, and see how the Lord has his friends who stay with him in his needs.</margin>

Now they give the Sacrament upon this reception. They eat at home, mixing things together—that is, they eat a "breakfast" <note>original: "fürstücke"; refers to eating a common meal or snack before the ritual, which the author sees as a distraction or a return to old habits.</note> beforehand. One contemplates worldly things; another, something else—his money, goods, interest, and fields, or children—and thus they remain unchanged in their old sins. For just as their hearing of the Word of God is, so also are their fruits and thoughts. They "whip" themselves <note>An idiom for a brief, forced performance of piety.</note> a little in the church, but outside, whenever an **opportunity** <note>original: "Occasiones"</note> arises, they dwell on these [worldly] things. And thus they forget the appointed times of Christ. <margin>the second part</margin>
As such, they have played games with the flesh and blood of Christ.
The highest thing in the Lord's Supper is that we do away with "love in the mouth" <note>Empty talk or superficial piety.</note> and drive everything into the hearts of men. Therefore, the right order is that those who wish to proclaim the death of Christ to the unbelievers come together and eat in their houses with one another, breaking the bread; at the end, they bless the Lord; they then eat his body and drink his blood, and sing the Lord his song of praise, after which follows the keeping of his commandments. Stand in every word, and proclaim

Therefore, the wise have a hunger only for righteousness on earth, solely in the body and blood of Christ, in which the spiritual follows, so that we may all be one and remain like Christ. May God graciously help us in this. Amen.

# ON THE ETERNAL LIMBO
## and the perpetual New Man of the second creation,
### from Christ the son of GOD.
<note>original: "DE LIMBO ÆTERNO." In Paracelsian philosophy, the "Limbo" refers to the "great reservoir" or the primal matter from which all things were created—the matrix of the universe.</note>

All philosophers who have been enlightened in the **Light of Nature** <note>The "Light of Nature" (Lumen Naturae) refers to the innate human capacity for reason and the understanding gained by observing the natural world, as distinct from the "Light of Grace" given through revelation.</note> have taken it upon themselves to describe the natural moisture of all things, their powers, and their works. In the same way, those who have sought to attribute natural virtues to me have also faced no small amount of opposition. For one who is knowledgeable in natural things finds it hard to leave them; the longer he researches and delves into them, the more gently he is led to investigate and follow them. Therefore, he not only loves them dearly but is driven to love them for eternity, until he realizes and can regard God. But what of it now, even if one searches through the entire <term>philosophy</term> <note>original: "phiam," an abbreviation for *philosophiam*.</note> of all natural things and brings them all to a correct understanding? He will still find that the whole of Nature is mortal and subject to all corruption. 

Now, whoever considers this rightly (as is proper), the gains of the <term>physician</term> <note>original: "physico." In this era, a "physicus" was a student of nature or a doctor of medicine who understood the physical world.</note> are diminished, even if he loves nature; for death is terrifying not only regarding man (however gruesome he appears in it!) but also in all things that are adversely shaped and felt by what is closest to them, feeling how pale death is. Thus, the philosopher also gains another mind, no longer to merely follow or pursue Nature, but he begins to investigate the mortal part which is *not* subject to death. This is now the true philosophy. 

In the meantime, it is my intention to describe those eternal things and powers that live within the troubled, mortal chest, which are without any death. For even if these are founded as entirely mortal in the Light of Nature, there is still a remnant <note>original: "Best," likely meaning "Rest" or the "finest part."</note> for death; the burden that remains dead is buried. Therefore, it is highly necessary for us to investigate the **eternal light** that remains with us even in death, and we with it, and how we may attain an immortal lot after this life. This is the philosophy of the fruit of **rebirth** and eternal joy. 

Before the calculation <note>Likely referring to the biblical genealogy or the timeline of history.</note>, since the creation of the first man, children have split into many ways and fallen from much understanding, taking up other things that they did not learn from their parents. The cause is that in many, the eternal has been abandoned, and nothing has been gained for the soul. Both think the body and soul are one thing and thus die together. And not only is there this error, but many more have come among men, which are not necessary to describe. 

But despite all that, the Light of Nature gives a demonstrable essence in man, both in the body and also in a mortal part. For when we consider man’s beginning, that he was formed after the image of God, that same image must be immortal and constant, and rule all things <term>firmamentic</term> <note>original: "firmamentisch," referring to the influence of the stars and the celestial sphere.</note>, <term>elemental</term> <note>original: "Elementisch," referring to the four physical elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note>, and divine over humanity.

## Little Book on the Sacrament of the Body of Christ <note>original: "corporis Christi"</note> to be Received for Salvation <note>original: "seligkeit"</note>

<margin>The first point of the sermon</margin>
First, we must know the reason why Christ our Lord commanded us to eat his body and drink his blood, and why he placed salvation so completely in the partaking <term>partaking: *Nießung*, specifically the spiritual or physical consumption of the Eucharist</term> of his body, flesh, and blood. And it is indicated therein that he shall live eternally and remain in Him—that is: God the Father and Christ in him—who eats his flesh and drinks his blood. Although it is often shown by what means and ways one comes to salvation, and one is shown after another, yet none is separated from the other. They are all the same path and nothing more than: whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved; whoever loves God and his neighbor as himself, he shall be saved. As in: Blessed are the poor in spirit. Blessed are the meek. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of Christ's name. Blessed are those who weep and those who bear suffering. Blessed are the merciful and many other glorious ones. Therefore, it is first necessary to know what is the right way to salvation.

You should understand at the outset that there is only a single way: but the fruits that proceed from salvation <term>salvation: *Seligkeit*, meaning both blessedness in this life and eternal salvation</term> are manifold. One fruit is gratitude, another is weeping, another is righteousness, and so on through all the others. Yet these first fruits are not fruits of repentance that belong to Heaven, such as, for example, the works of the poor. There it is rightly understood that through poverty one becomes saved. Rather, it is a matter of faith that one keeps the commandments of one's own accord as if they were not commanded, having been given by God only to point out hard hearts. (**For the law is not laid down for the righteous man** <note>original: "Iusto n: nō ē Lex posita"; a reference to 1 Timothy 1:9</note>). Blessed is he who loves God and firmly thanks Him as His child. We should understand this in three ways, and notice how I compare these three things. For whoever loves these three things with all their strength and senses, and their neighbor as themselves, that person is saved. For this reason, what was charged to you in the Old Testament is not taken from the commandments, but from the faith of the New Testament. From this flows the love for God, and it is said outwardly: (**For the good hate to sin out of love for virtue; the wicked, out of fear of punishment.** <note>original: "Oderunt n: peccare boni Virtutis amore, Mali, formidine poenæ"; a common moral maxim</note>) The commandment presses upon the Jews, but not upon the believing Christians. And because they do not fulfill that same commandment out of faith in the acceptance of the New Testament, it is a way to salvation for them. For the same flows alone from faith. Thus, there is also the way that is believed and grasped: that the child becomes saved. For from faith flows the love for God and the neighbor. From love flows the work of good fruits, which a saved man must and will have within him. Therefore, it follows from this that no one can or may be saved unless he be born a second time in the truth.

The first birth gives you the body, blood and flesh, bone, marrow, hair, eyes, memory, voice, and sensitivity. Likewise, the understanding of earthly things, the wisdom of the world, cleverness, pride <term>pride: *Hochart*, a term for arrogance or high-mindedness</term>, and the like. These all come from our natural fathers and the light of nature. They are inherited from us and are natural. Therefore, these things do not help at all in the matter of salvation. For they are not there for the purpose of winning salvation: but only to recognize or endure the "forest fire" or "land-fire" <note>likely a metaphor for the trials, passions, or temporal destruction of the earthly world</note>. But whoever wishes to be saved must be born a second time—not from his mother and his father, but from Christ. For salvation is in Him, and not in the flesh of the mother. And in the same way as a person is born from his mother into this world, so he is also born through Jesus Christ into Heaven. And though this is a difficult concept, everyone who wishes to be saved must recognize it, upon the loss of their very salvation.

I indicate first that man should come to have his part with the Spirit. Rather, he must be born of two fathers: from one into the world, and from the other into salvation. First, mark me in this way, by the traces left behind: how we are all born as men according to the flesh. And just as all men are in this world through Adam, their first father, so also must whoever wishes to be saved in the future be born again a second time here in this world out of Christ. It follows then that without the Spirit of God, without His blood and flesh, no man can or may come into this world. So

Just as without the flesh and blood of Christ—the other, heavenly Adam—no person can come to heaven. Therefore, there are two of all births: the one into this world, and the other into heaven.

You should understand these two births in this way: just as we are born from Adam into this earthly world, so in the same way we are born from Christ to heaven in death. For whoever wishes to be a child of Christ must be born for that purpose, so that Christ may be his Father; and this happens in no other way than through that very same birth. Thus it is to be understood: He is the Father and the flesh of all His children, where He gives birth to them for eternity with His blood and flesh.

And so the second birth is through Christ, because He held the Last Supper—for which He so heartily longed—and ate with His disciples; there He gave them His flesh and blood to eat and to drink. In this eating, they were born for the second time. This is the second birth of the children of God out of Christ into the Kingdom of God, for which (as stated above) He so heartily longed.

Therefore, the institution of the Last Supper declares this: That Christ gave to the disciples in the bread that which is released from it, and in the wine the same, etc. And it was not commanded in the Spirit alone. For in our flesh and blood, the second birth must happen: and it happens through Christ, just as through the seed of man. And just as the seed of Adam has born all men from Adam, so Christ, through His flesh and blood, has born all a second time who are ordained for salvation <term>salvation: *Seeligkeit*, implying both eternal life and the state of being "blessed"</term>. 

Whoever does not have this birth will not be saved. That is: he cannot be saved, just as a natural man cannot be made without a natural seed; so also no one can be saved without the flesh and blood of Christ. Herein is the reason to place great importance on the second birth. For Christ did not intend to redeem anyone other than His children; no one else. Thus, as one is His child, he is redeemed. We hear further that the institution of the order of baptism makes one saved, even then. He tells His disciples that the use of bread and wine—alongside the power of the work, and these are the words—is truly His body and blood, and that these are firmly fed to the communicants to eat and to drink. Thus He still does today; out of truth, it will continue on His side until the end of the world. He distributes to all believing people, through the power and working of His Spirit’s word, from that same one body and blood which He offered up on the altar of His cross and shed for the forgiveness of our sins. By this, He incorporates us as members of His body, possesses us, cleanses us, and preserves us for eternity. Although He sits in heaven at the right hand of God, He is not far from our life. Therefore all believers, as Paul says, are **flesh of His flesh and bone of His bone.** <note>A reference to Ephesians 5:30, used here to emphasize the literal, substantial union between Christ and the believer through the sacrament.</note>

Since He now separates these foods from one another—the food for the belly and the eternal food—He gives them by the hand of the Son of Man. For this reason, He considered Himself the Son of Man, so that you might understand the way it works. Thus, this food must be a different kind of food and contain more than just bare bread. Namely, it is the **flesh** of which He says, "This is [my body]." and even if it is not visible like the blessed Adam, it is nonetheless invisible like the soul, which is the man himself.

> **What shall we do, that we might work the works of God?**

This is a question from common people to such a man—namely, what must one do to become the person they ought to be? A person concerning the right within them, which has been placed there whether from the mother’s womb or from man, regardless of how humble they might be. They asked what they should do so that they might perform the **works of God**. They understood it this way: the "works of God" are the forgiveness of sins and other similar tasks to be fulfilled, which a human being cannot achieve, but only God alone. For what is it to build a house if no one is inside it? Is it not simply the work or the building of a man? Yes. So it is also with the Son of God: the more one believes in Him, [the more the house is filled]. Therefore, God’s work is this: that we believe in His Son. The Son is the work, as are all those who believe in Him. For they are made of the Son—His body, blood, and flesh. Therefore, if we believe in Him, we fulfill the will of God. That is now His entire work: the Son, and those who belong to the Son, His own and His chosen.

To maintain **eternal food** <note>original: "Ewige speise"</note> within a human being is a most wonderful thing, because we are all mortal. ### Jesus then said to them: "Truly, truly, I say to you: It was not Moses who gave you the bread from Heaven; but my Father gives you the true bread from Heaven."
<note>original Latin: "Dixit ergo eis JHESUS Amen Amen dico Vobis. Non Moses dedit panem de Celo: Sed pater meus dat vobis panem de Celo Verum." (John 6:32)</note>

Moses gave this bread, but where did he get it? Namely, from God. Thus Moses gave it, and God did not want Moses to say he had it from himself, despite the honor and the praise. For God works in many ways through His servants. But the bread that Moses gave, he did <unclear>certainly</unclear> not have from himself, nor from any human source. For Christ is God, and He gave both. How much more then is the bread of life than that of Moses, who was only a man, acting as a servant.

### For the true bread of God is he who comes down from Heaven and gives life to the world.
<note>original Latin: "Panis n. [namque] Verus ejus de Celo descendit, et dat Vitam mundo." (John 6:33)</note>

Therefore He speaks: the bread is God's, not Moses'. It was not done to serve the honor or praise of the servant, but for God Himself. For He alone is the one to whom the honor and praise belong. It is God's bread, not Moses' bread—bread that has descended from heaven. And that same manna <note>OCR reads "mamma," a common transcription error for the miraculous "manna" provided to the Israelites in the desert</note> fell from heaven and was <unclear>provided</unclear>. Yet that was not from the same heaven from which Christ descended. But the bread that has descended from Heaven—the true Heaven—gives life to the world. What is meant by "the world"? Not only the Jews, but also the heathens. Not only Greeks, but today also Germans. That is what "the world" means, to which this bread—so gloriously described—gives a <term>reward</term> <note>original: "lohn"; in this theological context, it refers to the gift or spiritual fruit of eternal life</note>. For it is not intended for the Jews alone; for they would not be even a fifth part of those who are meant. By "the world," however, all people are understood, through and through. Therefore, this bread (the Word) surpasses the bread of the Jews.

<note>original Latin: "Dixerunt ergo ad eum Semp. [Semper] da nobis panem hunc." (John 6:34)</note>

Therefore, notice that the human heart is changeable and wavers if it is not established and set by God. Otherwise, the devil runs in and intervenes, even if a person possesses good understanding. [As a measure of hope], on the <unclear>other side</unclear>, free will is recognized—whether one holds to the teaching or does not. One might be inclined to believe in God or not. But Scripture has grasped the concept of free will in this way: birth brings a person to where they are. Whether one is wise or simply God's creature, they are like captives in His hand. But Scripture speaks of a free will in the sense that a cause might change a person inwardly. At one time it stands, at another it does not. So it is with these Jews: previously they were against Christ, but now the Spirit has worked a change <note>original: "and lunge," likely "Wandlung" or transformation</note> in them, and now they want the bread all the time.

<meta>This page continues the theological commentary on the Gospel of John. While the previous page focused on the Bread of Life discourse in John 6, this page transitions into a broader defense of John the Evangelist’s unique spiritual authority and his specific role in explaining the "New Birth" and the "New Creature."</meta>

# CONCERNING THE LORD'S SUPPER <note>original Latin: "DE COENA DOMINI"</note>
### Chapter: Gospel of John; and this is the 7th point in the sequence

John the Evangelist has introduced a Gospel and a chapter out of his own spirit, which he received from God. In that same spirit, he grasped the high teaching of the beginning of the <term>other creature</term> <note>The "other creature" or "new creature" refers to the spiritual person born again through Christ, as opposed to the natural "old" person.</note>, from whence they come and where they took their beginning. Now, this description is necessary because John is an interpreter of the Lord and has expanded upon his other spirit. For previously, he spoke much regarding the second birth, and yet he did so alone. Thus, John has now added his own power to it and has given the most concerning Christ according to his spirit—how he is in him and he is in us. This was done so that he might make us partakers, through the teaching of the words, of the teacher of the <term>second birth</term> <note>Refers to the concept of being "born again" as discussed in John 3.</note> and the Mediator, of whom Christ spoke to Nicodemus.

If John had not written of the second birth and the teaching of the other creature and left it behind him, we would have no certainty of the second birth according to his spirit, from the number of writings of those who would also have given the most regarding what they held concerning it. What John held in this matter is that which we are to mostly accept. Thus, he ordained his spirit and interpreted this. Therefore, we should all rightly recognize this spirit of this man, who was sent from God for our sake. For he is such a man who provides us with help and teaches and interprets in this way. Therefore, he was a man as well as a human Christian spirit; his understanding should also proceed, and we should hold ourselves firm in that way, learning and having faith, just as this Evangelist—out of his own spirit, like a man gifted by God—intended and desired to instruct.

For his wise teaching is from this Evangelist, as a man sent from God, not distorted. Rather, it is well said: it is of God’s Holy Spirit. Therefore, we should accept the last chapter of the Evangelist John with great understanding. For there he concludes a noble, wise teaching. For this reason, he is rightly a noble one among all the Evangelists. For none among all the Evangelists flew higher in the spirit than he, the Evangelist John; he wrote even more than all of them. For he concludes here the greatest point of the <term>New Birth</term>, which is the greatest nobility here, which we must lay in our faith; upon this, it must be set and established. And if this first point is not brought home to us, then we lose all our things in a single stroke. Such is solely the body that we have from Christ. If we do not have that same body, then all our hope is gone.
