# On the 3rd Chapter of the Gospel of John, verse 3.

## Unless one is born again, etc. <note>original Latin: "Nisi quis renatus fuerit denuo &c."</note>

Here Christ rejects the birth of Adam from the Earth as a creature that you should no longer be, and says thus: that all those who are to come into the Kingdom of God or Heaven must be born anew, that is, from above. <margin>Note: Bodily</margin> graciously <note>The German "lieblich" (graciously/pleasantly) may also imply "leiblich" (bodily) given the marginal note, suggesting the new birth is a tangible transformation.</note> into another creature. For the first [birth] is worth nothing; it is lost and brought to nothing. Therefore, another birth must be there, and that same birth is from above. 

Thus Christ gives us to understand that we should not regard our descent from Adam—of flesh and blood—for it is all nothing before God. Instead, we should strive only for this: that we be born from above, and think purely of no father or mother. Nor should we take comfort in anyone, nor rely or hope in anything, except for this second birth. 

However, this is not to be understood otherwise than that we must, above all things, have a body for **salvation** <term>salvation: "Seligkeit," referring to eternal blessedness or the state of being saved</term>. Only then are all our things forgiven. Therefore, it is best to consider how we are born: in the same way that a human being is first born naturally as a natural human being, and thereafter has the strength and power to act as a human being. But if he is not born as a human being, then everything following will fail and be nothing. 

It is the same for those who wish to live a Christian life in the teaching, commandment, and love of God: that life must arise for them out of the body from which it may spring. If he does not have that same body, then all he does is in vain. Therefore, Christ sets here at the very beginning the start of salvation; that is solely the first article of the birth, which makes **repentance** <term>repentance: "Buß," the turning of the heart away from the world toward God</term> into a Christian. 

That same birth comes from above. It also deals with heavenly things! For otherwise, there is no house, no God anymore who calls to man from Heaven or may have him, except for us Christians, by reason of the second birth which we have. For those from the Earth are only from the Earth; those from Heaven are from Heaven.

## He cannot see the kingdom of God. <note>original Latin: "Non potest videre regnum Dei."</note>

Although man was placed into paradise according to the Creation, he was afterwards taken and cast out. Since God has now thus sent his friend <note>Likely referring to Christ as the "friend" of humanity or the mediator.</note> a second time into his creature in the course of time, who takes from Heaven to man, He had to be outside of paradise. Because this has occurred, Heaven is closed off further, so that God makes no more creatures from the Earth—not as his [other] creature. Rather, only what he creates anew must be from Heaven, and must be from his seed. Because of this, no one can be a friend of God anymore who enters his kingdom, which has been opened through repentance. 

For he must first have Heaven pure and clean for his flesh; therefore no one enters into Heaven unless he be of the body from Heaven, that is, born from Heaven. From that same body, no friend shall be commended to God the Lord anymore— <note>The sentence is interrupted as the page transitions to the next scripture verse.</note>

Jesus answered: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God." <note>original Latin: "Respondit Jhesus. Amen, Amen dico vobis, Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non pt [potest] introire in regnum Dei."</note> Here Christ reveals how we are to be born: not out of the nature of Adam, but out of two things—that is, out of the water and the Spirit. The water is now the conception through Christ; in that same name the Father baptizes, who has done this. He who is thus baptized, that is water, and the Spirit of God comes over him, and he is born anew; and the sin of Adam is [washed away], which is the second birth of man. Here is the Mother in whom man must be born a second time; and not in the natural mother, but in water and Spirit. Here he must be dead [to the world] and be Spirit. At best, man's mother is the Earth. For out of the Earth he was made. She is now his mother, and is not taken after the first death—she who was made from Adam’s rib <note>A reference to Eve</note>. Instead, he is understood here as coming from the mother Earth. Thus, the other mother here, as we receive her, is the water and the Spirit. Therefore, for our sake, the same Christ was baptized. He baptizes now in the same water he was baptized in, so we find ourselves in the second birth. In the same way that a child lies in the mother's womb and seeks nourishment from the **placenta** <term>placenta: "Placentt," used here as a biological metaphor for spiritual nourishment during the "gestation" of rebirth</term>. In this way, one is drawn and born out of the water; that is now the other mother into whom we must enter. He says here that the highly-rich, the wise <note>The original "weise" may mean "wise person" or "manner/way"; the author likely plays on both meanings</note> are born from above; here they will not see the Kingdom of God [otherwise]. From this, understand that baptism is from above, not from man, but from God, therefore it is specially fulfilled. The wise in baptism take the means of the second birth from above, and thereafter the Spirit is added. 

Now the Spirit of which he speaks is the Spirit Christ mentions that makes one alive; that is, just as Christ was conceived and born of the Virgin through the Holy Spirit—and that is the Mother Maria—so in the place of Mary will be what lies in the water. That is now the baptism which stands in Mary's place. Just as Christ was conceived in the appearance of the Virgin and became flesh and blood, so we become the flesh and blood of Christ through the Holy Spirit in baptism. For the Spirit in baptism gives the nourishment of flesh and blood from above, like a mother. Why then does it follow that the wise have these two: the baptism from above as a mother, and the Spirit carries them? And they have thereby the Spirit, the <unclear>head</unclear> New Man, born from above, and both are one word. For baptism is a word of Christ. Therefore baptism is as he instituted it to be baptized.

## That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. <note>original Latin: "Quod natum ē ex carne Caro ē. Quod natu est ex spiritu spiritus ē."</note>

<margin>JOHN 3.</margin>Yes, there are two births: the one out of the flesh and the other out of the Spirit. That which is out of the flesh is out of Edom <note>The author likely uses "Edom" (the descendants of Esau) as a symbol for the carnal, earthly man in contrast to the spiritual chosen ones.</note> from Adam; it remains flesh and is flesh. But that which is born out of the Spirit, that is spirit. Now the Spirit has become bodily blood and flesh within us. Therefore, we must not lie about what we are born as according to nature. For the flesh is like the grass <note>A reference to 1 Peter 1:24: "All flesh is as grass."</note>. Rather, it is what we have attained from the Spirit—that is, through the Holy Spirit through whom Christ became blood and flesh, through the blood and flesh that was conceived by the Holy Spirit. Also, that we all are from the New Father. Otherwise, we cannot truly say in the "Our Father": Our Father. Only if it is the case that we are His sons, and that we rightly believe in the Son, may we say:

->Our Father.<-

Only those can truly speak, truly say "Our Father," who are born from the Spirit a second time. That springs from what Christ says: "My Father." Because He is born of God through the Word that became flesh. In that same Word, we also become flesh and blood—those of us who are born out of that same Word, which is out of that same Spirit. These are the daughters and sons of brotherly love <note>original: "Filiae et Filij philadelphi," using the Greek term for brotherly love.</note>, that is, true siblings and brothers <note>original: "germani et fratres"</note> of Christ; they are true and not mere echoes of Christ. And these blessed ones, I say, may now say:

->O Our Father<-

In spirit and in truth. And these are the true worshipers; for this is how the Apostles were taught to pray, because they had become flesh and blood out of the Spirit. Thus we also should pray—not like the mockers <note>original: "Amen," likely a scribal error or specific local term for those who say 'Amen' without faith.</note> who make much chatter but are unconcerned. For they are not from God, from the True One, in that they are not children of the body from the Spirit; therefore they do not belong to Christ. Consequently, they lie when they say "Our Father." This applies to all Jews, Heathens, Calvinists, Arians, Baptists, etc. <note>The author provides a list of groups they consider "unbelievers" or heretics who cannot truly pray the Lord's Prayer.</note>

But whatever remains out of God works visibly, well, and perfectly; for just as the light surpasses the darkness, so also those who are of God surpass those who are not of God.

# Concerning the Gentile Maiden

<margin>John 4:13</margin>

> Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst forever. This story concludes with this: that Christ turned the Gentile woman <note>The "Gentile maiden" or "Heathen lady" (heidnischen fräullin) refers to the Samaritan woman at the well.</note> away from the darkness of the four elemental waters <note>referring to the physical world composed of earth, air, fire, and water</note> which she had held onto until now, [showing her] the eternal spring. # ON THE LORD'S SUPPER
<note>original: "DE COENA DOMINI"</note>
### FROM
# OTHER GOSPEL
<note>original: "DE COETERIS EVANGELII"</note>
### authors.

Dear reader, in this book you should take note of how, until now, the interpretation of several of Christ’s words has turned out—misunderstood, and not grasped according to the actual content of Christ’s text. Namely: When Christ was tempted to have bread made out of stones. The answer then was that man should live not by bread alone, but by every word that proceeded out of the mouth of God. Now, bread and the Word are one food. There, a twofold creature <note>The "twofold creature" refers to the human being as both a physical and spiritual entity, requiring both physical and spiritual nourishment.</note> is understood. Also, when Christ says, "False prophets will arise, who will say, 'I am Christ.'" That is He. Believe it not. Such things have all spread among the false prophets, so that each one has cast suspicion upon the other, and no one wanted to be the false prophet.

# Then if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’ do not believe it <note>original: "Tunc si quis vobis dixerit Ecce hic ē Christus nolite credere"</note>

Since Christ warns so strictly in this chapter how false prophets will come and will say "here is Christ, there is Christ," yet you must not believe it. He says further on: now it is necessary to weigh this well, for much depends on it. First, what this means: that if it were truly Christ, and I should not believe it—and if Christ had said "do not believe it"—then such a thing could not be. But they, the false prophets, say "believe, there He is," so they must indeed be lying. For God speaks and is also the truth; what God says, His Word itself confesses from His own mouth. Whenever a man speaks, it rests only on his own wit and cunning.

Now, here is a short report: believe in this way. Man holds his body to be from the Earth; from that perspective he says, "here is Christ, there He is," or wherever he happens to have Him. Now it is found, however, that the body of Christ is also with us; and that Christ is also with us, but not in one single manner—that is: in one form or also one kind of way, or in one single thing. Rather, His body is with us, just as it is proven, and Christ is also with us. And it is also proven that His body is with us, which is true. For He has given us the power 
<margin>John 1:12</margin>
to become children of God, that is: out of the Word that became flesh
<margin>John 1:14</margin>
and is flesh. For this He has given power. And since we are to have the soul dwelling within us, we use and benefit from it in the <term>Holy Supper: the Eucharist or Lord’s Supper</term> for Him, in remembrance. 

Thus, God the Father has marked and designated the bread—firstly the bread—as a Heavenly Bread leading to Him, to eternal life. Therefore, we have an "own body" and it is with us; just as we also have that which is the counsel of Nature, so it remains with us. And it is created for us along with its fruit, and they cannot be left behind; indeed, even before she (that is, when Adam was whole) could not exist without it. Therefore, He is also for us in Christ the "true marriage," that is, the <term>New Creature: the person spiritually reborn through faith</term>.

Also, Christ is indeed with us. For He had promised us and said that where two are gathered in His Name, He would be the third among them.

Thus also the keys are in us, and it is His hand—we have them. And He remains in us. Therefore, He has given them to us. He is the Lord, I am the servant; what He has to do, God binds and looses! For even if God gives us a power or authority, it is nothing other than that He might also be near to us. For that is the same. If He is not there, then no power holds Him. He must not be Himself alone: Therefore, He has given Himself to us, and we have Him essentially—His body, His blood.

But what is it if we do not have the Spirit (which is God)? That is: Himself. Where then shall we go with the body, if He Himself is not there? Into eternal damnation. Every word of God must be there, which has proceeded out of His mouth; otherwise, nothing is perfectly there. For what does it profit me if Christ gave me the keys, and He were alone and not with me? He wants to have such unity with me, between Him and us, according to the contents of His <term>Testament</term> <note>original: "Testament"; referring to the New Covenant established at the Last Supper</note>, namely that He be in us, and we in Him. Thus the key is there; now He is also there, as a Spirit and as God. And as we enjoy His Body and His blood, He is also bodily and spiritually with us. What is it that I have His Body in my hand, His blood in the <term>chalice</term> <note>original: "Kelch"; the cup used in the Eucharist</note>, and yet do not have Him? That is, not having His Spirit. Therefore, where one says: "There He is! In the field He is! In the bread He is!"—do not believe it. For there will be false prophets and false Christians, such that no one can say, "There is Christ." For He is a spirit; even if He is already in the midst of us, who sees Him? No one.

->Amen<-

Therefore, accept nothing else, but mine alone.

## DECLARATION OF THE LORD'S SUPPER.
<note>original Latin: "CŒNÆ DOMINI DECLARATIO."</note>

Here, in the description of my intention regarding the explanation of the Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ, it is first most necessary to describe its fruitfulness <note>The "fruitfulness" refers to the spiritual benefits and transformative power the believer receives from the sacrament.</note>, to describe the manner of understanding it, the cause—how it is to be grasped rather than suppressed—and how it is not to be an excess. And when this has been recounted, we shall then proceed to explain the text, as its nature will require. Just as we are born from Adam to death in the flesh here on earth, so we are born from Christ through His flesh and blood to eternal life in heaven. --- And just as the condition in Adam [leads] from the soul's own power and decree to a mortal or perishable life, so also we establish and achieve from the flesh and blood of Christ that the soul bears no debt or obligation [preventing] eternal life. As in Adam, the soul dies the eternal death along with the mortal flesh: so the soul unites itself with the body of Christ through His flesh and blood for eternal life. --- And just as the human soul without the flesh of Adam is alone and is nothing: so also that same soul without the flesh of Christ is nothing in eternal life. For the soul and the body on earth constitute one thing, and not two <unclear>both</unclear>. This is a mortal <term>conjunction</term> <note>original: "Coniunctio," a term used in both alchemy and theology to describe the joining of two distinct substances into one.</note> where what the one is, the other is also. For in Adam the body is [mortal], therefore the soul has become mortal within it, because it was married to the mortal and harmful flesh of the outside and thus also enclosed in death. But if it is to be fed by the earth, it must be lovely; if the dead [soul] wishes to have life, that happens through an immortal flesh and blood. Since we do not have this from Adam, it had to happen through Christ alone, whose flesh and "earth" <note>The author uses "earth" here to refer to the material substance of the body.</note> within us turns the earth of our bodies and souls toward eternity. Just as no one is redeemed through Adam, nor lives after death [by his own power]: so no one [comes out] of their sins through him, for through Adam [none have] come before the face of God so that their soul became blessed in the old flesh of Adam—as we say rightly and truly of what happened to the soul. That which is so blessed has all occurred through the death of the body and soul of Christ. For the body was given from Christ, outside of whom no one has ever become blessed or holy. And it cannot be otherwise, unless our <margin>B.C.</margin> soul be lovely married to the blood and flesh of Christ: otherwise NB. <note>original: "NB," an abbreviation for "Nota Bene," meaning "Note Well" or "Take notice."</note> there is no salvation in us. In this discourse, Paul concludes that there is but one food—the food in Heaven and on Earth. For God wills to have one Will in both, in Heaven and on Earth: And whoever does not will this, he does not receive Christ, according to which he is against Christ.

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of John 6, specifically addressing the tension between the physical "flesh" of Christ and the "Spirit." The previous page established that the Lord's Supper must be understood in a heavenly, rather than a purely natural or "Jewish" literal sense. This page clarifies that while the physical flesh of Christ is the vehicle for salvation, it is only through the Spirit (faith, hope, and love) that the sacrament becomes life-giving.</meta>

...food, the Lord's Supper, the wine and its use. So know now that flesh is a food, and a drink or beverage—as has been stated here. 

But now, the flesh is of no use, or worth nothing; it is the Spirit that gives life. <note>The author is quoting and interpreting John 6:63: "It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh is of no avail."</note> If you know that Christ’s flesh is worth nothing, then what of the flesh that has redeemed us from eternal death? That flesh is of great worth and is highly useful, and it must be within us (under penalty of losing our salvation) as has been proven until now. But as for the statement that the flesh is of no use, but rather the Spirit gives life; it is understood in this way:

In this, we also take that which becomes wine, which is intended for the Lord's Supper. However, the Spirit would not have salvation—that is, he would not be among the elect <note>The "elect" refers to those chosen by God for salvation.</note>—if the eating and drinking, as we ourselves eat it here, were useful for nothing other than the physical act without the Spirit. If that were so, then all the godless would be saved simply by the eating, even without the Spirit. 

What is the Spirit? It is our faith, love, and hope in Christ. We must have this, for it is what makes us alive; yet it does not do so without the flesh and blood of Christ, but rather *with* the flesh and blood. Just as the flesh by itself is never useful if the Spirit is not there, so too the Spirit is of no use without the flesh and blood of Christ. For it is from that flesh—from Christ alone—that the Spirit (that is, our faith) is established. Thus God the Father had previously...

<margin>The inner light</margin>

Therefore, we should rightfully place all our trust, comfort, and hope in and through the flesh and blood of Christ alone. And by no means should we let the errors remain which falsely point us toward our own sinful flesh. 

We must not eat the flesh of Christ in such a disordered way as if it were mere human flesh (like the <term>Capernaiten</term> <note>The "Capernaiten" or people of Capernaum refer to those in John 6 who were horrified by Jesus's words because they interpreted "eating his flesh" in a literal, cannibalistic sense.</note>, or those about whom the Apostle Paul complained in his epistle, saying they did not discern the body of the Lord). That is eating flesh merely to fill the belly. Instead, we should eat with the Spirit, as Peter, John, Philip, and the others did; they ate it and had the Spirit with them. 

That is to say: they had faith, love, and hope. The Jews <note>In the polemical language of the time, "the Jews" often symbolized those who cling to a literal or "carnal" interpretation of scripture rather than a spiritual one.</note> had none of these, and therefore they ate only the bare flesh and drank the blood. Therefore, Paul also says: *Let a man examine himself*, lest he eat judgment unto damnation <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:28-29 regarding the proper preparation for Communion.</note>; let us ensure that such a thing does not happen to us. 

This means that the physical act is not sufficient without the Spirit—that is, without the Holy Spirit, who teaches us and gives us understanding of the correct use of this healing food, rather than following our own blind, natural spirit. Therefore it is written further: **My words are Spirit, and they are life.** <note>Original Latin/German: "Meine wort seindt Geist, und seindt leben," quoting John 6:63.</note>

This means: I also give my body and my blood with the hand. But if my word were not there and did not come to it, what would the altar be? Therefore, my word makes alive that which the hands and the mouth grasp. For the bread and the wine would remain mere bread and wine, but the word of God that enters into them gives them life. For His words are Spirit, which [govern] all things...

...thing, the Life that gives life. For you know that nothing lives without the Spirit of God; whatever does not have the Spirit does not live. Now, concerning this word of mine that I speak to you now: that same word is Spirit and Life. That is to say, the Spirit is the life, and my word is that same Spirit. Therefore, I am the Bread that has come down from heaven. And unless it be the case that one eats [merely] as a fleshly act, you will have no life in you through the Spirit. Therefore, understand that when He says, "I am the bread," etc., He means that you should eat this, my flesh, and drink my blood. 

Thus, the word is Christ Himself, and it is the flesh of that being which must be eaten by those who wish to have eternal life. And they must have it with the Spirit, because the word of God is the life itself. For that person has not received [the sacrament] who has received damnation and not life in the eating—namely, receiving the flesh alone. For the flesh is of no use without the Spirit, which is hoped for in the word of God, so that it becomes living, just as Adam did at the word "Let it be" <note>original: *Fiat*, the Latin command from the Creation story in Genesis: "Let there be."</note>. 

Therefore, no one comes to Christ unless the Father gives him that life which is in the word. And He further grants the wisdom to understand that this is truly His bread—that is, His flesh which He sent to the Cross. And it is the bread which He gave in the Lord’s Supper <term>Nachtmal; the German term for the Last Supper or Communion</term>. Therefore, you chosen ones of God in Christ, judge now whether John, in this chapter or in his entire Gospel, is like the other three Evangelists <note>The "other three" refer to Matthew, Mark, and Luke, the Synoptic Gospels.</note>. 

And although he did not include the [narrative of the] Lord’s Supper within it—rather [speaking of it] before it occurred—yet the formal words of institution <note>original: *formalia institutionis*; the specific liturgical words used to consecrate the bread and wine</note> are seen more clearly here than in the accounts of the Lord's Supper itself. For the time [of the Last Supper] had not yet come then. Thus, John is like a preface and a pointer toward the Lord’s Supper, just as John the Baptist <note>original: *Johannes Baptista*</note> was a forerunner of the Lord Christ. And he was a preparation and a teacher for all believers, for this speech allows the Lord’s Supper to be understood subsequently. 

And that which is spoken secretly <note>or "mystically"</note> in this place is surely God’s interpretation. And that which God the Father spoke in the institution <note>original: *institutione*</note> is preached—this is the secret interpretation. And although I initially spoke as if John's account of the Lord’s Supper stood more fully there: understand it no differently than if I were to say that John the Baptist is indeed not Christ, but John nonetheless spoke of Christ, and pointed Him out and proclaimed Him; and he is the prophet who pointed to Him with the finger of God. 

In this way, John the Evangelist <note>original: *Johannes Evangelista*</note> is, in the matter of the Lord’s Supper, an interpreter, leader, and predecessor, and not a witness to the institution of that same Testament <note>The "New Testament" or "New Covenant" established at the Last Supper.</note> like the other three Evangelists. For as truly as Christ at that time [intended] the labor of His poor ones in the land who take the testimony here, the Lord’s Supper was not yet instituted or begun, as it is properly recounted by the others.

# Interpretation of the Text of St. Paul

> Behold, I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you. That the Lord Jesus, on the night in which he was betrayed, took bread, and giving thanks, broke it and said, "Take and eat, this is my body which is given for you." <note>original Latin: *Ecce accepi a domino quod et tradidi vobis. Quoniam Dominus Jhesus in ea nocte qua traditus est accepit panem, Et gratias agens fregit 7 dixit Accipite 7 manducate hoc e corpus meum quod pro vobis traditur.* This is 1 Corinthians 11:23-24.</note>

Paul has diligently taken it upon himself to describe and explain the Lord’s Supper <term>Nachtmal; the German term for the Last Supper or Holy Communion</term> for this reason: so that he might rebuke those who fail to understand this article of faith and instead bring them into the true faith. He ultimately intends for us to understand that we have there the Body of Christ and His Blood according to the explicit words of Christ. Furthermore, he does not wish to seek after other interpretations in his writings, but rather he maintains and recounts the events in order. He does this for the better and certain comfort of our conscience, so that there should be no doubt in this matter.

He did not boast of this account but simply set it forth more clearly, namely, so that the words of Christ might be easier to understand. Now, he remains focused on the blessing and thanksgiving of Christ and the breaking of bread, unswervingly interweaving these with the same words found in the accounts of the three **Evangelists**, **Matthew, Mark,** and **Luke**. He also says based on this: "As often as you do this, do it in remembrance of me." 

From this, the following words are further to be understood: "As often as you do this, you shall proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes in his *glory* <note>original: *Gloria*</note>." In this way, the [accounts of the] **Evangelists** are understood through **Paul** in this passage. As often as we do this, we should proclaim and remember the death of the Lord. This is the "remembrance"—that we should continue to do as He did until He comes again in His *glory*. That is to say, when we shall see Him in His Father’s Kingdom, where He will come in praise and we shall go to Him. 

From this, know that we should celebrate the Lord’s Supper according to our current state here [on earth]. And when this celebration has taken place, we should proclaim the death of the Lord in our hearts, not just with the mouth. This serves as a memorial to Him—that He suffered and acted solely for our sake and for our benefit, just as the words of the <term>Augsburg Confession; the primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church (1530)</term> state. 

And it was ordained as a Testament <note>The author uses "h.e.", likely for the Latin *hoc est* (that is), to clarify the nature of the sacrament</note> to receive His form, Body, and Blood in His time. The doing of this is commanded by the power of Divine authority, in a manner unlike the other commandments. This is the highest commandment regarding the Lord’s Supper: that one must next praise and proclaim the death of the Lord. For this is how Christ wants it: that we eat His supper and then must proclaim His death.

Therefore, such people are identified by their "folly" <note>original: "stoltit," likely meaning a combination of prideful negligence and senselessness</note>. Therefore, to prevent such self-will and "mad-headedness" <note>original: "dollen kopff"</note> and to avoid their arrogance, Paul commanded that they should be together and wait for one another. In this, he gives us to understand the order of Christ: that they all ate together, were taught publicly, and ate publicly. This is Redemption. Afterward he says: "As the Meal is also better, as soon as I return, I will also set you in order." <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 11:34: "The rest I will set in order when I come."</note> Therefore, in no way or manner should an individual's own way or opinion be allowed—such as a "dream" that might occur to someone. Rather, we should be of one mind, one opinion, and one way, undivided. For division is of the Devil and not of God; He wants us to have unity of heart, as in Heaven so also on Earth. <meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s explanation of the Annunciation (Luke 1:35), moving from the limits of human reason to a detailed alchemical and theological description of how the "Power of the Most High" interacts with the Virgin Mary, whom he identifies as the "Middle Body."</meta>

The fire has over-flamed Mary, the Middle Body <term>Mittel Corpus</term>; but the Spirit and the power of the Most High comes upon <note>original Latin: *supervenit*</note> her—meaning it comes upon her and into her.

->Thus, in this work, there are three laborers or persons, and only one patient<- <note>In the language of alchemy, the "laborant" is the active worker or agent of change, while the "patient" is the substance or subject that undergoes the transformation.</note>

The first Laborer is the Most High, from whom all power comes. The second Laborer is the power of the Most High, His eternal birth. The third Laborer is the Holy Spirit, as it were of Adam’s [spirit]. He who comes upon <note>original Latin: *IS qui supervenit*</note> her. The patient is the Middle Body, who offers herself and willingly suffers <note>In this context, "suffers" means to undergo or receive the action of the laborers.</note> everything they wish to do and accomplish with her. Namely, the Pure Virgin Mary <term>Virgo</term>, the chosen wall, and also the Middle Body of the Virgin from which Christ—the Son of the Most High—shall be born.

<margin>Note well: what the Power of the Most High is.</margin>

For the Most High is the Father; He will not let such works of birth happen without His overshadowing from the Middle Body. He is the one who, with His ignited over-flaming in the Middle Body, awakens the spirit. And that same spirit also joins with His Spirit, and with His power awakens and makes alive again the dead, dried-out Body, so that a new birth may be driven forth. And He illuminates a mute, darkened mind, and so forth.

This birth must have a body, because it is born from a body. It must also have a spirit, because it is born from the spirit. It must also have a soul, because her Middle Body, from which it comes, was an anointed part. And yet, above all this, He must be the Son of the Most High; therefore the Son of the Most High was born from the beginning, and afterwards in the Middle Body became an out-birth <note>German: *außgeburtt*; a term Paracelsus uses for a manifestation or a product of a specific process.</note> into a spiritual and divine nature; and from the Middle Body He was embalmed and saturated, and thus a whole Christ—who is true God and Man—was made therefrom.

But what is the "middle" and the "patient," Mary? A pure, chaste Virgin, whom no man had ever defiled. For in this seed, the sperm and the juices <note>original: *Samen und Sosen*</note> shall be those that come correctly and directly, not from something foreign. This birth proceeds only from one Matter <term>Materien</term>, which has no man except its own spirit and soul <term>Animam</term>. To understand this: the Spirit "coming upon" her <note>original Latin: *Spiritus superveniens*</note> is God the Most High, who joins this part as her husband; and from the seed she conceives, and further bears the Son of the Most High. And because He is a Son of the Most High, the highest eternal flesh <term>carnem eternam</term> lies within Him. For no one comes to the Father, but by the Son.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the mystery of the Incarnation, shifting focus to the nature of God as an unapproachable "consuming fire." It explains why the divine must be veiled or "overshadowed" to interact with humanity without destroying it, drawing parallels between biblical appearances of God and the alchemical process of spiritual "hatching" or maturation.</meta>

...to come as a human, he would have been turned to ash in an instant. For God is a **consuming fire**. Therefore, no creature can stand before him, whom he would not immediately, in the first moment or blink of an eye, reduce into their **first matter** <note>original: "suam primam materiam"; the fundamental, undifferentiated substance from which all things were created</note> and bring to nothingness. For he made all things out of nothing; therefore, he can also bring all things to nothing in a moment with his supernatural, fiery essence.

For this reason, the assembly of Israel did not want to, nor could they, hear His fire any longer. For when He is present, the element most like Him is stirred; then heaven and earth tremble, and it appears as if everything is about to collapse into a heap. But so that this does not happen, and His creatures might persist until their enlightenment, He comes **overshadowed** <note>original: "obumbratus"; covered or veiled so as not to overwhelm the world with His full glory</note> in another form. 

For when He spoke with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, they saw Him like another human; and He wrestled with Jacob, just as one fighter forces another. But [He appeared] in the person and form that Christ later took upon Himself over two thousand and sixty-two years ago. Otherwise, His essence is far too fine, far too subtle, and of such a penetrating power that it would **resolve** <note>Break down into component parts</note> everything in an instant—whatever encounters His divine essence as it is in itself—just like a fiery thunderbolt that consumes the iron and blade within the scabbard, yet no one knows where it comes from, and the scabbard remains whole. In the same way, God would consume man if he were to see Him before his enlightenment and **regeneration** <note>The process of spiritual rebirth through which a person is made capable of enduring the divine presence</note>. 

Therefore, it is magnificently and beautifully said: **And the power of the Highest shall overshadow you** <note>original: "Et virtus Altissimi obumbrabit tibi"; the Latin text of Luke 1:35, referring to the Holy Spirit coming upon the Virgin Mary</note>. That is to say: the power of God will come to you very gently, that is, under and within a cool cloud, to surround and illuminate you, passing through you with a sweet gaze. 

And thus the Spirit of God will "warm-hatch" these stones into action. This is now a magnificent work, in which such powerful **laborers** <note>Likely referring to spiritual or alchemical forces that work upon the soul or "matter"</note> stand and have much to do, using all their **Secrets** <note>original: "Archana"; hidden spiritual or medicinal powers or "mysteries"</note> in the **Star** <note>original: "Astrum"; the celestial influence or the internal "guiding light" within a substance</note> and mastery. *   1 part of this liquor

*   1/3 part <term>crab’s eyes</term> <note>original: "Krabbs augen" (Oculi Cancrorum); not actual eyes, but calcium carbonate stones found in the stomachs of crawfish, used as an antacid</note>

...should do? Since Nature herself is accustomed to giving birth to such things within the passages of the earth. And thus the Artist <note>In alchemy, the "Artist" is the practitioner or chemist</note> requires nothing more than to be a tool of the Lord; here the instruments hold the form of the Creator. In this artificial driving [process], however, where a perfect body is necessary, it must be kept according to the proportion of the external, movable mass, so that the internal, active heat, power, and virtue within that mass do not exceed the required amount in the slightest—neither too much nor too little—as shall be explained in detail in its proper place. For if it has too much heat, the form of life dies from it and leaves behind its empty fire and body; if it has too little warmth, it will not move toward life or growth. 

For that which is internal is an unmanifested essence within a fiery substance, which stands before us and is rightly called the power of Nature. For she is the spirit and form of all metals, which enlivens all bodies and makes them perfect. And if the Artist does not recognize this power, he may wander in many errors before he might reach a <unclear>mark</unclear> <note>original: "merck"</note> here.

For such light cannot be seen until the hidden things are clearly placed into the light and the <term>elements</term> <note>original: "Elementa"</note> are overturned. Therefore <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: Our spirit, which makes all <term>metallic bodies</term> <note>original: "corpora metallorum"</note> alive or is also a natural fire, cannot be seen unless the Father’s spirit and Light make one alive.

# Water of Salt

Take <note>The symbol $\mathcal{R}$ stands for the Latin *Recipe*, meaning "Take."</note> dissolved salt or the purest substance and place it over pieces of ignited **Ashes** <note>original: "Cinerum"; likely hot coals or embers used to provide steady, indirect heat</note>, which you will afterward distill just like **strong water** <term>Strong Water</term> <note>original: "aquam fortem"; typically nitric acid, used by alchemists to dissolve silver and other metals</note>. Afterward, remove the **phlegm** <note>The "phlegm" is the watery, inactive portion of a distilled liquid</note> from this water using a **Water Bath** <term>Water Bath</term> <note>original: "Balneum"; also known as a *bain-marie*, a vessel of hot water used for gentle heating</note>. In a kettle vessel, add as much pure salt as the first three fingers can grasp <note>A standard alchemical measurement for a large pinch</note>. Distill this through a sand bath. This will very easily dissolve gold, other metals, and all other minerals.

Take 2 pounds of common salt and 1 pound of **Ore** <note>original: "Ores"; could refer to a specific mineral or a misspelling of *oris* (gold). Given the context of "dew," it may refer to a mineral salt</note>; use this or **dew** <note>original: "roris"; dew was often collected by alchemists as a "pure" celestial water</note>, or an equal amount of the same. Afterward, distill with a very strong fire. A **dead vapor** remains in the bottom, looking like <unclear>glass</unclear>, and finally <unclear>then</unclear> <unclear>it will be resolved</unclear> into <unclear>salt</unclear>. And there is more: This dissolves gold and leaves a very white particle in the bottom which is <unclear>hard</unclear>, in which there is no longer any **tincture** <note>The "tincture" is the essential color or "soul" of the metal; if it is gone, the metal has been "stripped" of its essence</note>. It works much more slowly than the first recipe.

If **verdigris** <note>original: "viride æris"; the green pigment or crust that forms on copper</note> is dissolved in strong water and distilled from it, and if gold and four <unclear>vegetable parts</unclear> reside in the bottom through it [represented by the symbol for ☉ Gold], this water is made equal and increases the color of the gold.

->Method of dissolving ☉ Gold & ☽ Silver.<-

Take the best **sublimated mercury** <term>Sublimated Mercury</term> <note>original: "☿ sub."; likely corrosive sublimate or mercuric chloride</note> along with a fourth part of salt. Place it in a vessel to be resolved into a water, which you then distill through the medium of strong water that has had its first phlegm removed. The **Mercury** [☿] dissolves itself by **putrefying** <note>The process of "rotting" or breaking down matter through gentle, moist heat</note> for several days. Then, when the water is distilled over a very slow fire, an **oil** will remain in the bottom <margin>b. r. i. q. rs. b. g :</margin> <note>These marginal abbreviations likely refer to specific lab instructions like "balneum" (bath) or "recipe"</note>. Dry this with an equal weight of **Oil of Tartar** <term>Oil of Tartar</term> <note>original: "olei tartari"; a concentrated potassium carbonate solution</note> when it begins to become rough; let it be elevated and **calcined** <note>Reduced to a powder through high heat</note>. If it is then melted, you will distill the first material and then dissolve it in lukewarm water; you will have your mercury.

### Vision in a Water-filled Vial

Let the vial <note>original: "Viola," likely referring to a glass vial or vessel, though the word also means the violet flower</note> be emptied, and let it likewise be cleaned with care. Afterward, let it be pierced on the top at its mouth in the shape of a cross, and fill it with honey-water salted during the day. While speaking, make a circle upon the table toward the west and place the vial there; then let it remain so through the entire night. Then, in the morning around the eighth hour, pour in olive oil through a funnel <note>original: "falsigidium," likely a corrupted term for a funnel or filter</note> to the depth of two fingers. Place incense, in large enough grains, [therein]. From this [will come] two reflections; and while carrying [the vessel], you should have a virgin boy born of a legitimate marriage bed. Bind his eyes with a single linen cloth. Then purify yourself with an unsheathed sword and pass it around <note>original: "perure," perhaps a corruption of "perire" (to go around) or "per-urere" (to burn through/purify with fire)</note> three times, and in the same way, pass it around the vial three times.

Then say: I conjure over you, O Messiah Gashadgadah Kuka . . . . . . . . . . Zagragan . Uba . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Metra . . . Binm . . . . . . . . . num . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Joseph. In the name of *Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh* <note>original Hebrew: **אהיה אשר אהיה** ("I am that I am")</note>, the Cherubim, Jah, Ekateriel, Sabaoth, and Uriel.

<margin>the commands</margin>
And by the nine swimmers <note>possibly referring to the celestial spheres or specific stars</note>, and by the ten Biblical [names/commandments], and by the 72 Angels standing in the wheel <note>original: "rotula," the *Schemhamphorasch* or the 72-fold name of God</note>, and by the Sun ☉ and the Moon ☾, and by the bond upon which the whole world hangs, and by the four corners of the world, and by all the Angels—Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, and Uriel—that you may come immediately into this vial and into this linen cloth (or mirror and such things), that you may show this cloth to me [without] fear, but show the triple-holy things of this number.

Similarly, strike the left hand three times. Above the crown of the head, hold [the vessel] at the doorway and strike yourself with a <unclear>mace</unclear> or [staff]. "Messiah, enter this limit." Then loosen the linen cloth from the eyes of the boy and let him say to you "Messiah, enter into this vial" three times; and then he will appear to the boy. You then say to him: I conjure you, Messiah, to show the boy by your own Gashadgadah <note>evidently a secret name or power associated with the spirit</note>, by Heaven and earth, by mountains and valleys, by sea and marshes, and by all things that are in them and above them, so that immediately and without delay you show me <term>N. N.</term> <note>the placeholder for the name of the person or thing the practitioner wishes to see</note> etc.

Then you shall dismiss him so that he does not descend into your dwellings and does no harm to any creature, but let him leave immediately and [peacefully] <note>original: "paroch," likely a corruption of "parochus" or a dismissal formula</note>, then he will vanish. And in the aforesaid house, there may be fire and a lamp in the likeness of <unclear>Gashalli</unclear>; let the sword be put away, etc.
